From weighted paraboloid restriction to kk-stars and distance graphs

Tainara Borges, Yumeng Ou, Marcus Pasquariello T. BorgesDepartment of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA Email address: tborges@sas.upenn.edu Y. OuDepartment of Mathematics, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA Email address: yumengou@sas.upenn.edu M. PasquarielloDepartment of Mathematics, Brown University, Providence, RI 02912, USA Email address: marcus_pasquariello@brown.edu
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In this paper, we study pinned kk-star distance sets associated to compact subsets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2. For pins x1,…,xk∈Ex_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in E, the pinned kk-star distance set is

Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E)={(|x1−x|,…,|xk−x|):x∈E}⊂ℝk.\Delta_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}^{k\text{-star}}(E)=\{(|x_{1}-x|,\dots,|x_{k}-x|):x\in E\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{k}.

We obtain improved Hausdorff-dimension thresholds on EE guaranteeing that pinned kk-star distance sets have positive kk-dimensional Lebesgue measure. The main analytic input is a reformulation of the connection, first observed in [17], between kk-stars in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and pinned dot products on the paraboloid in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. In our framework, L2​(ℝk)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{k}) estimates for the densities of pinned kk-star distance measures are reduced to a weighted Fourier extension estimate for the paraboloid whose weight is defined explicitly in terms of Frostman measures on EE. For 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, this yields the threshold

dim(E)>α+​(n,k):=n2+n​k+k2​n+1=n+k−12+14+2​k+14​(2​n+1).\dim(E)>\alpha_{+}(n,k):=\frac{n^{2}+nk+k}{2n+1}=\frac{n+k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2k+1}{4(2n+1)}.

Using the graph-building machinery of [1], our positive-measure results for kk-stars can be used as building blocks for finite distance graph configurations with prescribed pins. As a consequence, we improve the best-known positive-measure thresholds for pinned kk-simplices in every dimension n≥3n\geq 3 and for necklace graphs (cycles) in every dimension n≥3n\geq 3.

We further prove nonempty interior results for kk-stars. In the special case k=1k=1, corresponding to pinned nonempty interior of the distance set Δx​(E)={|x−y|:y∈E}\Delta_{x}(E)=\{|x-y|\colon y\in E\}, we use a sharper argument to improve the pinned nonempty-interior thresholds of [3] in all dimensions n≥4n\geq 4.

1. Introduction and main results

A central theme in geometric measure theory is to understand when a fractal set determines many geometric patterns. The prototypical example is the Falconer distance problem: given a compact set E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, one asks how large dim(E)\dim(E) must be in order to ensure that

Δ(E)={|x−y|:x,y∈E}\Delta(E)=\{|x-y|:x,y\in E\}

has positive Lebesgue measure. A more refined version is the pinned distance problem, where one fixes a pin x∈Ex\in E and studies

Δx​(E)={|x−y|:y∈E}.\Delta_{x}(E)=\{|x-y|:y\in E\}.

Here the goal is to find dimensional hypotheses guaranteeing that Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) has positive measure for at least one, or for many, pins x∈Ex\in E, which in particular implies positive measure for Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E). The Falconer distance set conjecture [9] says that, for the distance set to have positive Lebesgue measure, it suffices to assume the Hausdorff dimension of E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} to be larger than n2\frac{n}{2}.

The Falconer distance problem has seen major progress in recent years. In the plane, Guth, Iosevich, the second listed author, and Wang [14] proved that if E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} and dim(E)>5/4\dim(E)>5/4, then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that the one-dimensional Lebesgue measure of Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) is positive:

ℒ1​(Δx​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{1}(\Delta_{x}(E))>0.

In dimensions n≥3n\geq 3, the best currently known threshold is due to Du, the second listed author, Ren, and Zhang [5], who proved the same conclusion under the condition

dim(E)>n2+14−18​n+4.\dim(E)>\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{8n+4}.

Very recently, Liu [20] proved the Falconer distance conjecture in the plane under additional assumption of regularity of the set EE.

One may also ask for the stronger conclusion that distance sets have nonempty interior. In the unpinned setting, Mattila and Sjölin [22] proved that

dim(E)>n+12\dim(E)>\frac{n+1}{2}

implies int⁡(Δ⁡(E))≠∅\operatorname{int}(\Delta(E))\neq\emptyset. The pinned nonempty-interior problem is more delicate, and the best known thresholds remain higher than their unpinned counterparts. Peres and Schlag [26] showed that, for n≥3n\geq 3, the condition

dim(E)>n+22\dim(E)>\frac{n+2}{2}

guarantees the existence of x∈Ex\in E such that int⁡(Δx​(E))≠∅\operatorname{int}(\Delta_{x}(E))\neq\emptyset. This was recently improved by the first two authors of the present paper, together with Foster and Palsson [3]: they proved that the threshold 7/47/4 suffices in the plane, and that in dimension n=3n=3 the Peres–Schlag threshold can be lowered from 5/25/2 to 12/512/5.

More generally, one may study distance vectors associated to finite graphs whose vertices are sampled from EE, with some vertices fixed in advance. In this paper, we focus on the pinned kk-star configurations, which play a fundamental role in the theory of general distance graphs. First, it is a natural generalization of the distance set, as the k=1k=1 case corresponds exactly to the aforementioned Falconer distance problem. Second, results of kk-stars can be used as building blocks to derive corresponding estimates for any pinned graph configurations. We give a more detailed discussion of this application towards the end of the introduction.

More precisely, by a kk-star we mean the pinned graph with k+1k+1 vertices {v1,…,vk,vk+1}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k},v_{k+1}\} where the first kk vertices are pinned, and the edge set is {(vi,vk+1):1≤i≤k}\{(v_{i},v_{k+1})\colon 1\leq i\leq k\}. See Figure 1 for a 77-star. The distance set associated with a pinned kk-star is then

(1.1) Δx1,x2,…,xkk−s​t​a​r​(E):={(|x1−xk+1|,|x2−xk+1|,…,|xk−xk+1|):xk+1∈E}.\Delta^{k-star}_{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k}}(E):=\{(|x_{1}-x_{k+1}|,|x_{2}-x_{k+1}|,\dots,|x_{k}-x_{k+1}|)\colon x_{k+1}\in E\}.

A simplified version of the main theorem of the paper is the following.

Theorem 1.1.

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set with Hausdorff dimension

dim(E)>α+​(n,k)=n2+n​k+k2​n+1=n+k−12+14+2​k+14​(2​n+1).\dim(E)>\alpha_{+}(n,k)=\frac{n^{2}+nk+k}{2n+1}=\frac{n+k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2k+1}{4(2n+1)}.

Then there exist pins x1,…,xk∈Ex_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in E such that

ℒk​(Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{k}\bigl(\Delta^{k\text{-star}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}(E)\bigr)>0.
Remark 1.2.

Observe that α+​(n,k)=n\alpha_{+}(n,k)=n when n=kn=k. The condition k<nk<n cannot be removed, since it was observed in [1] that a pinned kk-star result with nontrivial threshold is only possible in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} when n>kn>k. Moreover, the result is mostly interesting for k≥2k\geq 2 and n≥3n\geq 3, since when k=1k=1, the current thresholds for the Falconer distance problem are smaller than α+​(n,1)\alpha_{+}(n,1) [14, 5].

As far as we know, the study of the kk-star configurations was initiated fairly recently in [17]. And the main motivation was to understand the Falconer type problems for kk-simplices. Very recently, in [1], it was further observed that kk-stars can be used as building blocks to study any pinned distance graphs, which adds significant importance to the study of the kk-star problem. In fact, the graph building mechanism in [1] is quite delicate, and will need a stronger and more technical version of Theorem 1.1 as the building block. To state the full version of our main theorem, we first recall some definitions from [1].

Given a simple graph GG with vertex set 𝒱\mathcal{V} and edge set ℰ⊆2𝒱\mathcal{E}\subseteq 2^{\mathcal{V}}, pick a set of vertices to pin, 𝒫={v1,v2,…,vm}\mathcal{P}=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{m}\} where m≥0m\geq 0 (m=0m=0 corresponding to the unpinned case). Let 𝒱∖𝒫={vm+1,vm+2,…,v|𝒱|}\mathcal{V}\setminus\mathcal{P}=\{v_{m+1},v_{m+2},\dots,v_{|\mathcal{V}|}\} be the set of unpinned vertices. Then every edge can be identified with a pair (i,j)(i,j), some 1≤i≠j≤|𝒱|1\leq i\neq j\leq|\mathcal{V}|. We will further assume that no edge has been fully pinned, that is, 𝒫\mathcal{P} does not contain any pair of vertices vi,vjv_{i},v_{j} such that (i,j)∈ℰ(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}.

For distinct points x1,…,xm∈ℝnx_{1},\dots,x_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we define the mm-pinned GG-set of EE by

(1.2) Δ𝒫,x1,…,xmG(E):={(|xi−xj|)(i,j)∈ℰ:xm+1,xm+2,…,x|𝒱|∈E distinct}⊂ℝ|ℰ|.\Delta^{G}_{\mathcal{P},x_{1},\dots,x_{m}}(E):=\bigl\{(|x_{i}-x_{j}|)_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}}:\;x_{m+1},x_{m+2},\dots,x_{|\mathcal{V}|}\in E\text{ distinct}\bigr\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{E}|}.

In words, such a distance set captures vectors of edge lengths obtained by fixing the mm chosen pins in the graph at certain locations x1,x2,…,xmx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m} in EE, and by allowing the other unpinned vertices from the graph to be sampled anywhere in EE.

The notion of admissibility for pinned graphs was introduced in [1]. We recall it here.

Definition 1.3 (kk-admissible pinned graphs).

Let (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}) be a pinned graph with pins in 𝒫={vi}i=1m\mathcal{P}=\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{m}. For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, a pinned graph (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}) is kk-admissible if there is a way of listing the unpinned vertices vm+1,vm+2,…,v|𝒱|v_{m+1},v_{m+2},\dots,v_{|\mathcal{V}|} such that the back-degree is always bounded by kk, that is,

d<i​(vi):=|{u∈{v1,…,vi−1}:(u,vi)∈ℰ}|≤k,∀i>m.d_{<i}(v_{i}):=\big|\{\,u\in\{v_{1},\dots,v_{i-1}\}:\ (u,v_{i})\in\mathcal{E}\,\}\big|\leq k,\,\forall i>m.
Theorem 1.4 ([1]).

Let GG be a graph with vertex set 𝒱\mathcal{V} and edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Let 𝒫⊂𝒱\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{V} be such that no pair of vertices in 𝒫\mathcal{P} is connected by an edge in ℰ\mathcal{E} and denote m=|𝒫|m=|\mathcal{P}|. Assume that (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}) is a kk-admissible pinned graph. Let n≥2n\geq 2. Then, for 1≤k<n1\leq k<n and any compact set E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with Hausdorff dimension larger than n+k2\frac{n+k}{2}, there are distinct points x1,⋯,xm∈Ex_{1},\cdots,x_{m}\in E, such that the pinned distance set Δ𝒫,x1,⋯,xmG​(E)\Delta^{G}_{\mathcal{P},x_{1},\cdots,x_{m}}(E) as defined in (1.2) has positive |ℰ||\mathcal{E}|-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

The threshold n+k2\frac{n+k}{2} in the theorem above is intrinsically related to the previously best known threshold for kk-stars obtained in [17] and could be upgraded to the best thresholds for the pinned Falconer problem when k=1k=1.

Before recalling where the threshold n+k2\frac{n+k}{2} comes from, we will need a few more definitions.

Definition 1.5.

Given a compact set E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, an α\alpha-Frostman measure μ\mu on EE is a nonzero finite Borel measure supported on EE satisfying

μ⁡(B⁡(x,r))≲rα,for all ​x∈ℝn​ and ​r>0.\mu(B(x,r))\lesssim r^{\alpha},\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\text{ and }r>0.

By Frostman’s lemma [23, Theorem 2.7], such measures exist for every 0<α<dim(E)0<\alpha<\dim(E).

Definition 1.6.

Given a Frostman measure μ\mu supported on a compact E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and AA a Borel set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, denote by μA\mu_{A} the restriction of μ\mu to AA. That is, μA​(B)=μ⁡(B∩A)\mu_{A}(B)=\mu(B\cap A) for any Borel set B⊂ℝnB\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. If AA is compact set with μ⁡(A)>0\mu(A)>0, then the new measure μA\mu_{A} is a Frostman measure supported on AA.

Definition 1.7.

Let 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. We will say that a collection {E1,…,Ek}\{E_{1},\dots,E_{k}\} of compact sets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} is transverse if the following holds:

|x1∧⋯∧xk|≥cfor all ​xi∈Ei.|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\geq c\qquad\text{for all }x_{i}\in E_{i}.

Here |x1∧⋯∧xk||x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}| denotes the kk-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors x1,…,xkx_{1},\dots,x_{k}, viewed as vectors based at the origin. In particular, x1,x2,…,xkx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k} are linearly independent.

Definition 1.8 (Abundance of L2L^{2} pinned kk-stars).

Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be compact and let μ\mu be a finite Borel measure supported on EE. We say that EE has an abundance of L2L^{2} pinned kk-stars relative to μ\mu if the following holds:

For every collection of pairwise separated compact sets E1,…,Ek+1⊂E∖{0}E_{1},\dots,E_{k+1}\subset E\setminus\{0\} with μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0 for each ii and {E1,E2,…,Ek}\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{k}\} transverse, one has

(dx1,…,xk)∗(μEk+1)∈L2(ℝk) for μE1×⋯×μEk a.e. (x1,…,xk)∈E1×⋯×Ek,(d_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}})_{*}(\mu_{E_{k+1}})\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{k})\text{ for }\mu_{E_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mu_{E_{k}}\text{ a.e. }(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E_{1}\times\dots\times E_{k},

for μEi\mu_{E_{i}} as in Definition 1.6 and dx1,x2,…,xk​(y):=(|x1−y|,|x2−y|,…,|xk−y|)d_{x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k}}(y):=(|x_{1}-y|,|x_{2}-y|,\dots,|x_{k}-y|).

In the definition above, compact sets E1,…,Em⊂ℝnE_{1},\dots,E_{m}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} are said to be pairwise separated if, for each i≠ji\neq j, there exists ci​j>0c_{ij}>0 such that

|xi−xj|≥ci​jfor all ​xi∈Ei,xj∈Ej.|x_{i}-x_{j}|\geq c_{ij}\qquad\text{for all }x_{i}\in E_{i},\ x_{j}\in E_{j}.

Equivalently, since the sets are compact, they are pairwise disjoint with positive mutual distance.

Remark 1.9.

Whenever we say that there is an abundance of pins (x1,…,xk)∈Ek(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E^{k} with respect to μ\mu for which a given property holds, we mean the following: for every collection of pairwise separated compact sets E1,…,Ek⊂EE_{1},\dots,E_{k}\subset E with μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0 and {E1,E2,…,Ek}\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{k}\} transverse, the property holds for μE1×⋯×μEk\mu_{E_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mu_{E_{k}} almost every (x1,…,xk)∈E1×⋯×Ek(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E_{1}\times\cdots\times E_{k}.

With these definitions in mind, the result for kk-stars proved in [17] reads as follows.

Theorem 1.10 ([17]).

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be compact with dim(E)>n+k2\dim(E)>\frac{n+k}{2}. Let μ\mu be an α\alpha-Frostman measure on EE, where α>n+k2.\alpha>\frac{n+k}{2}. Then EE has an abundance of L2L^{2} pinned kk-stars relative to μ\mu. Consequently, there is an abundance of pins (x1,…,xk)∈Ek(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E^{k} such that,

ℒk​(Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{k}\bigl(\Delta^{k\text{-star}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}(E)\bigr)>0.

It was shown in [1] that a kk-star result with the L2L^{2} strength stated above transfers to positive-measure results for kk-admissible pinned graphs. Since improvements for kk-stars can lead to improved thresholds for Falconer type results for many interesting graphs, the main motivation for this work is to improve the dimensional thresholds in Theorem 1.10. Our main theorem is the following improvement, which implies Theorem 1.1.

Theorem A.

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set with Hausdorff dimension

dim(E)>α+​(n,k)=n2+n​k+k2​n+1=n+k−12+14+2​k+14​(2​n+1).\dim(E)>\alpha_{+}(n,k)=\frac{n^{2}+nk+k}{2n+1}=\frac{n+k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2k+1}{4(2n+1)}.

Let μ\mu be an α\alpha-Frostman measure on EE, where α>α+​(n,k).\alpha>\alpha_{+}(n,k). Then EE has an abundance of L2L^{2} pinned kk-stars relative to μ\mu. Consequently, there is an abundance of pins (x1,…,xk)∈Ek(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E^{k} with respect to μ\mu such that,

ℒk​(Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{k}\bigl(\Delta^{k\text{-star}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}(E)\bigr)>0.

The main analytic step in the proof of Theorem A is a reduction from pinned kk-star distance measures to weighted Fourier extension estimates for the paraboloid. For fixed pins, we rewrite the L2L^{2} norm of the density of the associated pinned kk-star distance measure in terms of the paraboloid Fourier extension operator evaluated along the linear span of the corresponding points on the paraboloid. This is the content of Lemma 2.8, which plays the role that Liu’s identity (see [18, Theorem 1.9]) plays in recent works on the Falconer distance problem.

In the case k=1k=1, where kk-stars reduces to the Falconer distance problem, Fourier restriction estimate has been a widely used tool in the study of the distance problem for decades. It is well known that (see for instance Wolff [28] and Erdoğan [8]), through the framework of Mattila integral, one can reduce the original unpinned Falconer distance problem to weighted restriction estimates. In the pinned case, a similar reduction was successfully achieved by Liu [18], where he established an L2L^{2} identity that directly links the L2L^{2} norm of the density of the pinned distance measure to the L2L^{2} norm of the Fourier extension of a function supported on the sphere. This identity opened the door to all the most recent improvement towards the pinned version of the Falconer distance conjecture, where the question is reduced to weighted restriction estimates for the sphere.

The key novelty of our method is that we establish a new L2L^{2} identity for all kk-stars (including the k=1k=1 case) that can serve a similar purpose, connecting the kk-star problem directly to a weighted Fourier restriction problem hence making it possible to introduce analytic tools into the study. Even in the case k=1k=1, such a connection to the weighted extension estimates for the paraboloid does not seem to have been observed before and brings new perspectives into the distance set problem.

Indeed, the new identity we established in the paper is distinct from the classical approaches in the following ways. First, unlike the classical approaches that reduce the problem in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} to a weighted restriction problem for the sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, our framework reduces it to a weighted restriction problem for the paraboloid in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. It is known that the paraboloid and the sphere display different behaviors in the weighted restriction theory (see e.g. [7]). Hence this new connection may bring additional insights into the theory of distance problems. Second, while the classical approaches reduce the distance problem to the Fourier extension of the Fourier transform of the Frostman measure, our framework instead turns it into the Fourier extension of the Frostman measure itself. In addition, this framework can also be more easily extended to the general kk-star case, whereas it’s unclear to us whether the approach via Liu’s identity could be used to study the kk-stars. More detailed discussions on these comparisons can be found in Section 4.

Another interesting feature of our proof is the role played by the averaging operator over a lower dimensional sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. It is well known that, in the k=1k=1 case, the pinned distance measure is naturally related to the spherical averaging operator where the sphere Sn−1S^{n-1} is centered at the pin. For k≥2k\geq 2, a similar averaging operator is brought into the picture where the sphere is of higher codimension and is jointly determined by all the kk pins. Such an operator seems to be intrinsically more difficult to understand than the standard spherical average, and we expect that improved understanding of it would shed new light on the kk-star problem.

As mentioned earlier, the role of Theorem A is broader than the kk-star configuration itself. Since it gives an improved abundance theorem for L2L^{2} pinned kk-stars, it can be used as the input in the graph-building framework of [1]. Consequently, Theorem A yields the following corollary for kk-admissible pinned graphs.

Corollary 1.11.

Let GG be a graph with vertex set 𝒱\mathcal{V} and edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Let 𝒫⊂𝒱\mathcal{P}\subset\mathcal{V} be such that no pair of vertices in 𝒫\mathcal{P} is connected by an edge in ℰ\mathcal{E} and denote m=|𝒫|m=|\mathcal{P}|. Assume that (G,𝒫)(G,\mathcal{P}) is a kk-admissible pinned graph. Then, for n≥2n\geq 2, 1≤k<n1\leq k<n and any compact set E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with Hausdorff dimension larger than

α+​(n,k)=n+k−12+14+2​k+14​(2​n+1),\alpha_{+}(n,k)=\frac{n+k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2k+1}{4(2n+1)},

there are distinct points x1,⋯,xm∈Ex_{1},\cdots,x_{m}\in E, such that the pinned distance set Δ𝒫,x1,⋯,xmG​(E)\Delta^{G}_{\mathcal{P},x_{1},\cdots,x_{m}}(E) has positive |ℰ||\mathcal{E}|-dimensional Lebesgue measure.

Thus, the weighted restriction estimates used to prove Theorem A translate, through the graph-building framework of [1], into improved Falconer-type thresholds for every kk-admissible pinned graph. Several special classes of graphs are of particular interest. In Subsection 1.2, we state several explicit corollaries about these graphs of our theorem. Specifically, we discuss cycles, also known as necklaces, and simplices, both of which have played a central role in previous work on Falconer-type configuration problems.

Theorem A also improves several of the area-vector thresholds obtained in [2]. The Jacobian method developed there transfers positive-measure results for pinned distance graphs to the corresponding vectors of triangle areas whenever the associated length-to-area map has full rank. Consequently, replacing the previous kk-star threshold n+k2\frac{n+k}{2} by α+​(n,k)\alpha_{+}(n,k) immediately improves the dimensional hypotheses for the area configurations treated there that are built from kk-admissible graphs. These include, for example, pinned fans, fish graphs, wheels, and circumscribed flowers, in the ranges where k<nk<n.

1.1. Nonempty interior results and dimension estimates for kk-stars

In addition to positive Lebesgue measure type results, our approach to Theorem A has the advantage that it can be readily adapted to study other related problems for the kk-star sets and beyond. Surprisingly, even in the k=1k=1 case (the Falconer distance set problem), it yields several new improvements of previously best known results.

For sets E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, rather than seeking dimensional thresholds that guarantee Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) or Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) have positive measure, one may ask for sufficient conditions ensuring the stronger conclusion that Δ⁡(E)\Delta(E) or Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) has nonempty interior. A classical result of Mattila and Sjölin [22] states that if E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} satisfies dim(E)>n+12\dim(E)>\frac{n+1}{2}, then int⁡(Δ⁡(E))≠∅\operatorname{int}(\Delta(E))\neq\emptyset. For the pinned analogue, Peres and Schlag [26] showed that when n≥3n\geq 3 and dim(E)>n+22\dim(E)>\frac{n+2}{2}, there exists x∈Ex\in E such that int⁡(Δx​(E))≠∅\operatorname{int}(\Delta_{x}(E))\neq\emptyset. Later, Iosevich and Liu [15] derived improved exceptional set estimate for the pinned nonempty interior problem in certain regimes and introduced a new method based on local smoothing estimates. More recently, these thresholds were improved and extended by the first two authors of this paper, Foster and Palsson in [3]. In particular, they proved that in the plane the same conclusion holds under the condition dim(E)>7/4\dim(E)>7/4, and that in dimension n=3n=3 the threshold can be lowered to 12/5=2.412/5=2.4. They also showed that, if the local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation were established for n≥3n\geq 3, then the threshold could be further reduced to n+22−12​n\frac{n+2}{2}-\frac{1}{2n}, representing an improvement of 12​n\frac{1}{2n} over the Peres–Schlag threshold.

The nonempty interior problem extends naturally to kk-star distance sets. When k=1k=1, this reduces precisely to the pinned nonempty interior problem for distance sets discussed above.

Question 1.12.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 and E⊂ℝn,n≥2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{n},\,n\geq 2. Under what hypotheses on the Hausdorff dimension of EE can one guarantee the existence of points x1,…,xk∈Ex_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in E such that

Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E):={(|x1−x|,|x2−x|,…,|xk−x|):x∈E}\Delta_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}^{k\text{-star}}(E):=\{(|x_{1}-x|,|x_{2}-x|,\dots,|x_{k}-x|):x\in E\}

has nonempty interior in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}?

To the best of our knowledge, apart from the case k=1k=1, this question has not been explicitly studied before. By adapting ideas from the proof of Theorem A, we obtain the first nonempty-interior thresholds for pinned kk-star distance sets with k≥2k\geq 2.

Theorem B.

Let n≥3n\geq 3 and 1≤k<n21\leq k<\frac{n}{2}. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set satisfying

dim(E)>α∘​(n,k):=n+2​k−12+14+4​k+14​(2​n+1).\dim(E)>\alpha^{\circ}(n,k):=\frac{n+2k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{4k+1}{4(2n+1)}.

Let μ\mu be an α\alpha-Frostman measure on EE, where α>α∘​(n,k)\alpha>\alpha^{\circ}(n,k). Then there is an abundance of pins (x1,…,xk)∈Ek(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in E^{k} with respect to μ\mu such that Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E)\Delta_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}^{k\text{-star}}(E) has nonempty interior in ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k}.

The condition n>2​kn>2k in the statement above is imposed to ensure that the dimensional hypothesis is nontrivial, that is, α∘​(n,k)<n\alpha^{\circ}(n,k)<n. So far, there isn’t a mechanism in the literature that allows us to transfer thresholds for nonempty interior of kk-stars to nonempty interior of kk-admissible graphs. In some cases, one can succeed in using the nonempty interior result for kk-stars to obtain nonempty interior for more complicated distance graphs. We will give an example in the next subsection by providing an application of the nonempty interior result for 22-stars to the nonempty interior of even necklaces.

For the case k=1k=1, which is of independent interest, we can further improve the threshold above by adapting ideas from [6]. In that case, we obtain the following.

Theorem C.

Let n≥3n\geq 3, and let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set satisfying

dim(E)>n2+34+34​(2​n−1)=n⁡(n+1)2​n−1.\dim(E)>\frac{n}{2}+\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4(2n-1)}=\frac{n(n+1)}{2n-1}.

Then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that Δx​(E)\Delta_{x}(E) contains a nontrivial interval.

Remark 1.13.

In the case k=1k=1, let us compare the thresholds in Theorem B and C with the previously best known ones in [3]. For all n≥5n\geq 5, the threshold in Theorem B is smaller than n2+1−12​n\frac{n}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2n}, which is the threshold that would follow from the argument in [3] and the sharp local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation. In all dimensions, the threshold in Theorem C is always smaller than that in Theorem B. For every n≥4n\geq 4, the threshold in Theorem C is smaller than what would follow from the argument in [3] and the sharp local smoothing conjecture. In n=3n=3, Theorem C recovers the same threshold 12/5=2.412/5=2.4 obtained in [3]. For n=2n=2, we obtain no information, so the threshold 7/47/4 in [3] remains the best.

When the dimension of the set EE is smaller than α+​(n,k)\alpha_{+}(n,k), Theorem A does not apply. However, our method can still be adapted to derive lower bounds for the Hausdorff dimension of the kk-star sets of EE in this regime. The exact statement of our result is given in Theorem 5.2 in Section 5. In the k=1k=1 case, such dimensional estimates for the distance set has attracted a great amount of attention in recent years and exciting new progress has been obtained via many different approaches ranging from Fourier analysis [19], projection theory [27], to computability theory [10]. We refer the interested reader to these works and the references therein for a detailed recount of the recent progress and state-of-the-arts results in different regimes. In the case k≥2k\geq 2, Theorem 5.2 seems to be the first of its kind. Just like the Lebesgue measure results, such dimension estimates for kk-stars also play a fundamental role in the theory of general distance graphs and can be used to derive similar results for kk-admissible graphs. For instance, as an application of the k=2k=2 case of Theorem 5.2, we obtain in Corollary 5.3, for the first time, a dimension estimate for pinned triangle sets. The proof is inspired from the work of the second listed author and Taylor [24], where a mechanism translating dimension estimates for pinned distances to chains and trees was established. However, the method in [24] was not strong enough to handle cycles.

1.2. Applications of Theorem A and Theorem B to cycles and kk-simplices

Consider the particular case in which the graph of interest is a cycle ClC_{l} with ll vertices. For even cycles, Greenleaf, Iosevich, and Pramanik [12] studied the constant-gap problem. More precisely, they proved that, if d≥4d\geq 4 and

dim(E)>d+32,\dim(E)>\frac{d+3}{2},

then the set of common edge lengths {t>0:(t,…,t)∈ΔCl​(E)}\bigl\{t>0:(t,\ldots,t)\in\Delta^{C_{l}}(E)\bigr\} contains a nontrivial interval. More recently, Iosevich, Magyar, McDonald, and McDonald [16] obtained an analogous result for 44-cycles in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} under the assumption

dim(E)>53−33712.\dim(E)>\frac{53-\sqrt{337}}{12}.

These results concern the constant-gap slice of the full cycle distance set. By contrast, our positive-measure result concerns the full set of edge-length vectors in ℝl\mathbb{R}^{l}.

Since cycles with no adjacent pinned vertices are 22-admissible, Corollary 1.11 implies the following result, which improves the threshold n+22\frac{n+2}{2} originally established in [1].

Corollary 1.14 (Improvement for ll-cycles).

Let l≥3l\geq 3. Let ClC_{l} be a ll-cycle graph with m≥0m\geq 0 pins listed in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, such that no pair of vertices in 𝒫\mathcal{P} shares an edge. Then, if n≥3n\geq 3 and E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact set satisfying that

dim(E)>n+12+14+54​(2​n+1),\dim(E)>\frac{n+1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{5}{4(2n+1)},

then the corresponding pinned ll-cycle distance set has positive ll-dimensional Lebesgue measure, in the sense that

OPENℒl​(Δ𝒫,x1,x2,…,xmCl​(E)))>0\mathcal{L}^{l}\left(\Delta_{\mathcal{P},x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m}}^{C_{l}}(E))\right)>0

for some x1,x2,…,xm∈Ex_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{m}\in E.

Another important graph is Kk+1K_{k+1}, the complete graph in (k+1)(k+1)-vertices, also known as a kk-dimensional simplex. In that case 𝒱={v1,…,vk+1}\mathcal{V}=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{k+1}\} and ℰ={(i,j):1≤i<j≤k+1}\mathcal{E}=\{(i,j)\colon 1\leq i<j\leq k+1\}, with associated unpinned distance set

Δk−s​i​m​p​l​e​x​(E):={(|xi−xj|)1≤i<j≤k+1:xi∈E​ for all ​1≤i≤k+1},\Delta^{k-simplex}(E):=\{(|x_{i}-x_{j}|)_{1\leq i<j\leq k+1}\colon x_{i}\in E\text{ for all }1\leq i\leq k+1\},

and pinned counterpart

Δx1k−s​i​m​p​l​e​x​(E):={(|xi−xj|)1≤i<j≤k+1:xi∈E​ for all ​2≤i≤k+1}.\Delta_{x_{1}}^{k-simplex}(E):=\{(|x_{i}-x_{j}|)_{1\leq i<j\leq k+1}\colon x_{i}\in E\text{ for all }2\leq i\leq k+1\}.

In the case k=2k=2, K3K_{3} is a triangle. The pinned distance set (with pin in x1x_{1}) in that case looks like

Δx1t​r​i​a​n​g​l​e(E)={(|x1−x2|,|x2−x3|,|x3−x1|):x2,x3∈E distinct},\Delta^{triangle}_{x_{1}}(E)=\{(|x_{1}-x_{2}|,|x_{2}-x_{3}|,|x_{3}-x_{1}|)\colon x_{2},x_{3}\in E\textnormal{ distinct}\},

and its unpinned counterpart is

Δt​r​i​a​n​g​l​e(E)={(|x1−x2|,|x2−x3|,|x3−x1|):x1,x2,x3∈E distinct}.\Delta^{triangle}(E)=\{(|x_{1}-x_{2}|,|x_{2}-x_{3}|,|x_{3}-x_{1}|)\colon x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}\in E\textnormal{ distinct}\}.

The study of triangle configurations realized in thin sets of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} has a rich literature, and it goes back to Greenleaf and Iosevich [13] who proved that ℒ3​(Δt​r​i​a​n​g​l​e​(E))>0\mathcal{L}^{3}(\Delta^{triangle}(E))>0 whenever E⊂ℝ2E\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} with dim(E)>7/4\dim(E)>7/4. That was improved to the threshold 8/58/5 by Greenleaf, Iosevich, Liu and Palsson in [11]. The group action method in that paper takes spherical-average decay inputs into dimensional thresholds for unpinned results for positive measure of kk-simplices, and it can be stated as follows.

Proposition 1.15 (Group action criterion given spherical-average decay input [11]).

Let n≥2n\geq 2. Assume that for every α\alpha-Frostman measure μ\mu on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} one has

(1.3) ∫Sn−1|μ^(Rω)|2dσ(ω)≲μ,ϵR−βn​(α)+ϵ,R≥1.\int_{S^{n-1}}|\widehat{\mu}(R\omega)|^{2}\,d\sigma(\omega)\lesssim_{\mu,\epsilon}R^{-\beta_{n}(\alpha)+\epsilon},\qquad R\geq 1.

for some βn​(α)>0\beta_{n}(\alpha)>0. Let 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Then, if E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is compact and

(1.4) α+1k​βn​(α)>n\alpha+\frac{1}{k}\beta_{n}(\alpha)>n

for some α<dim(E)\alpha<\dim(E), then

ℒ(k+12)​(Δk−s​i​m​p​l​e​x​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\bigl(\Delta^{k-simplex}(E)\bigr)>0.

Since [11] was published, improved spherical-average decay estimates have been proved in n≥3n\geq 3 by Du and Zhang [6], who obtained βn​(α)=n−1n​α\beta_{n}(\alpha)=\frac{n-1}{n}\alpha. Incorporating this improvement, the group action method from [11] leads to the following

Theorem 1.16 ([11],[6]).

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set with dim(E)>8/5\dim(E)>8/5 if n=k=2n=k=2 or

dim(E)>αDZ/GILP​(n,k):=k​n2(k+1)​n−1\dim(E)>\alpha_{\textnormal{DZ/GILP}}(n,k):=\frac{kn^{2}}{(k+1)n-1}

if n≥3n\geq 3, then ℒ(k+12)​(Δk−s​i​m​p​l​e​x​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{\binom{k+1}{2}}(\Delta^{k-simplex}(E))>0.

For the pinned counterpart, the following result was obtained in [17], which, to our best knowledge, is the best pinned kk-dimensional simplex result for k≥2k\geq 2 in the literature.

Theorem 1.17 ([17]).

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact with dim(E)>n+k2\dim(E)>\frac{n+k}{2}. Then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that

ℒ(k+12)​(Δxk−s​i​m​p​l​e​x​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{\binom{k+1}{2}}(\Delta^{k-simplex}_{x}(E))>0.

Since the complete graph on k+1k+1 vertices, corresponding to a kk-simplex, is kk-admissible even when one vertex is pinned, we can apply Corollary 1.11 to obtain the following improvement over [17].

Corollary 1.18 (New threshold for kk-simplices).

Let 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. If E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact set satisfying that

dim(E)>α+​(n,k):=n+k−12+14+2​k+14​(2​n+1),\dim(E)>\alpha_{+}(n,k):=\frac{n+k-1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2k+1}{4(2n+1)},

then there exists x∈Ex\in E such that one has positive measure of kk-simplices pinned at xx, namely

ℒ(k+12)​(Δxk​-simplex​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{\binom{k+1}{2}}\left(\Delta_{x}^{k\text{-simplex}}(E)\right)>0.
Remark 1.19 (Comparison with the unpinned simplex thresholds).

Since

Δxk​-simplex​(E)⊂Δk​-simplex​(E)\Delta_{x}^{k\text{-simplex}}(E)\subset\Delta^{k\text{-simplex}}(E)

whenever x∈Ex\in E, Corollary 1.18 also implies an unpinned positive-measure result for kk-simplices under the condition

dim(E)>α+​(n,k).\dim(E)>\alpha_{+}(n,k).

It is therefore natural to compare this threshold with the one obtained by combining the group-action method of [11] with the Du–Zhang spherical-average decay estimate [6], namely

αDZ/GILP​(n,k):=k​n2(k+1)​n−1.\alpha_{\mathrm{DZ/GILP}}(n,k):=\frac{kn^{2}}{(k+1)n-1}.

For n=2n=2 and k=2k=2, Corollary 1.18 does not apply, and the relevant unpinned triangle threshold is the GILP threshold 8/58/5. For n=3n=3, the GILP/DZ threshold is better for both k=2k=2 and k=3k=3: in particular,

αDZ/GILP​(3,2)=94<177=α+​(3,2),\alpha_{\mathrm{DZ/GILP}}(3,2)=\frac{9}{4}<\frac{17}{7}=\alpha_{+}(3,2),

while k=3k=3 lies outside the nontrivial range of Corollary 1.18.

In dimensions n≥4n\geq 4, there is a split. For 2≤k≤n−22\leq k\leq n-2, one has

α+​(n,k)<αDZ/GILP​(n,k),\alpha_{+}(n,k)<\alpha_{\mathrm{DZ/GILP}}(n,k),

so Corollary 1.18 gives the better currently available threshold for positive measure of kk-simplices. On the other hand, for k=n−1k=n-1 and k=nk=n, the GILP/DZ threshold is better. In the case k=nk=n, our pinned kk-star theorem is vacuous, since the nontrivial range for pinned kk-stars requires k<nk<n.

As a corollary of our new threshold for 22-stars, we improve the best known threshold for pinned triangles in all dimensions n≥3n\geq 3. We state this explicitly as a corollary.

Corollary 1.20.

(Improvement for pinned triangles) Let n≥3n\geq 3. For any E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with dim(E)>n+12+14+54​(2​n+1)\dim(E)>\frac{n+1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{5}{4(2n+1)}, there exists x∈Ex\in E such that ℒ3​(Δxt​r​i​a​n​g​l​e​(E))>0\mathcal{L}^{3}(\Delta_{x}^{triangle}(E))>0.

Remark 1.21.

The preceding corollary improves the pinned triangle threshold, but it does not close the gap between the best pinned and unpinned results in low dimensions. In dimension n=2n=2, the unpinned triangle problem has the nontrivial threshold 8/58/5, while no nontrivial pinned analogue is currently known. In dimension n=3n=3, our result lowers the pinned threshold from 5/25/2 to 17/717/7, but this remains above the unpinned threshold αD​Z/G​I​L​P​(3,2)=9/4\alpha_{DZ/GILP}(3,2)=9/4 obtained by group-action methods.

Moving on to applications of Theorem B, although the nonempty-interior result for pinned kk-stars does not currently feed into a general graph-building theorem for nonempty interior for distance sets of kk-admissible graphs, it can still be used as a building block in some specific configurations. We illustrate this for even cycles pinned at every other vertex, using the nonempty-interior result for 22-stars.

Corollary 1.22.

Assume n≥5n\geq 5, and let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} with

dim(E)>α∘​(n,2)=n+32+14+94​(2​n+1).\dim(E)>\alpha^{\circ}(n,2)=\frac{n+3}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{9}{4(2n+1)}.

For every l≥2l\geq 2, let C2​lC_{2l} be an even cycle with 2​l2l edges, and consider the corresponding pinned distance set with pins at every other vertex, namely

Δx1,x3,…,x2​l−1C2​l,l pins(E):={(|x1−x2|,|x2−x3|,|x3−x4|,…,|x2​l−1−x2​l|,|x2​l−x1|):x2​i∈E,∀ 1≤i≤l}.\Delta_{x_{1},x_{3},\dots,x_{2l-1}}^{C_{2l},\text{l pins}}(E):=\bigl\{(|x_{1}-x_{2}|,|x_{2}-x_{3}|,|x_{3}-x_{4}|,\dots,|x_{2l-1}-x_{2l}|,|x_{2l}-x_{1}|):\,x_{2i}\in E,\ \forall\,1\leq i\leq l\bigr\}.

Then there exists x1,x3,…,x2​l−1∈Ex_{1},x_{3},\dots,x_{2l-1}\in E such that

Δx1,x3,…,x2​l−1C2​l,l pins​(E)\Delta_{x_{1},x_{3},\dots,x_{2l-1}}^{C_{2l},\text{l pins}}(E)

has nonempty interior in ℝ2​l\mathbb{R}^{2l}.

Remark 1.23.

Nonempty interior for odd cycles is still out of reach with our methods. For example, a triangle is a 22-admissible graph, but it is not clear whether a nonempty-interior result for 22-stars necessarily implies a nonempty-interior result for triangle distance sets. We refer to [25] for an unpinned nonempty interior result for triangles with threshold 2​n3+1\frac{2n}{3}+1 in ℝn,n≥4\mathbb{R}^{n},\,n\geq 4.

Organization of the paper

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we reduce the kk-star problem in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} to a weighted restriction estimate for the paraboloid in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1}. In Section 3, we study the geometric and dimensional properties of the weights arising in this reduction. The proof of Theorem A is presented in Section 4. In Section 5, we prove Theorem B, the nonempty-interior counterpart of Theorem A, establish dimension estimates below the dimensional threshold in Theorem A, and illustrate how dimension estimates for 22-stars can be used to obtain dimension estimates for triangles. In the appendix, we adapt ideas from Du–Zhang [6] to prove Theorem C, and we also give an application of Theorem A to derive a discrete variant of it. To our knowledge, this seems to be the first result concerning pinned kk-stars in the discrete setting.

2. Reduction to Weighted estimates of the Paraboloid Extension Operator

In this section, we relate the key L2L^{2} integral of the density of a pinned kk-star to a weighted Fourier extension estimate for the paraboloid. Throughout the section, we assume that n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. We first introduce some definitions.

Definition 2.1.

Given points 𝒙=(x1,…,xk)∈(ℝn)k\bm{x}=(x_{1},...,x_{k})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{k}, we let A𝒙A_{\bm{x}} denote the affine span of the points x1,…,xkx_{1},...,x_{k}. In other words, A𝒙A_{\bm{x}} is the smallest affine subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} containing the points x1,…,xkx_{1},...,x_{k}, or equivalently,

A𝐱={∑j=1kλjxj:λ1,…,λk∈ℝ,∑j=1kλj=1}.A_{\mathbf{x}}=\left\{\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}x_{j}:\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}\in\mathbb{R},\ \sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_{j}=1\right\}.

In the same way that the distance map dx=|⋅−x|d_{x}=|\cdot-x| is closely related to the spherical average operator, the push-forward of d𝒙d_{\bm{x}} is related to a lower-dimensional spherical averaging operator. To define this operator, we make the following definitions.

Definition 2.2.

Let Aff⊂(ℝn)k\textup{Aff}\subset(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{k} be the set of points that are affinely linearly independent. That is,

Aff:={𝒙=(x1,…,xk)∈(ℝn)k:dim​(A𝒙)=k−1}.\textup{Aff}:=\{\bm{x}=(x_{1},...,x_{k})\in(\mathbb{R}^{n})^{k}:\text{dim}(A_{\bm{x}})=k-1\}.
Definition 2.3.

For 𝒙=(x1,…,xk)∈Aff\bm{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in\textup{Aff} and 𝒕=(t1,…,tk)∈(0,∞)k\bm{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{k})\in(0,\infty)^{k}, we denote

Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕):=Sn−1​(x1,t1)∩⋯∩Sn−1​(xk,tk).S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}):=S^{n-1}(x_{1},t_{1})\cap\cdots\cap S^{n-1}(x_{k},t_{k}).

In other words,

Sn−k(𝒙,𝒕)=d𝒙−1(𝒕)={xk+1∈ℝn:|xj−xk+1|=tj, 1≤j≤k}.S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})=d_{\bm{x}}^{-1}(\bm{t})=\{x_{k+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:|x_{j}-x_{k+1}|=t_{j},\ 1\leq j\leq k\}.

It’s a well-known fact that under the assumption 𝒙∈Aff\bm{x}\in\text{Aff}, Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}) is either empty, a point, or a (n−k)(n-k)-dimensional sphere (see [21] Theorem 2.1). Let D𝒙:ℝn→ℝD_{\bm{x}}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} denote the determinant of the Jacobian of the distance map d𝒙:ℝn→ℝkd_{\bm{x}}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{k}:

D𝒙(xk+1)=(det(∇d𝒙(xk+1)∇d𝒙(xk+1)T))1/2.D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})=(\det(\nabla d_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})\nabla d_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})^{T}))^{1/2}.

Note that ∇d𝒙​(xk+1)\nabla d_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1}) is the k×nk\times n matrix given by

(x1−xk+1|x1−xk+1|,…,xk−xk+1|xk−xk+1|)T.\left(\frac{x_{1}-x_{k+1}}{|x_{1}-x_{k+1|}},\dots,\frac{x_{k}-x_{k+1}}{|x_{k}-x_{k+1}|}\right)^{T}.

Therefore

D𝒙(xk+1)>0⇔rank(∇d𝒙(xk+1))=k⇔xk+1∉A𝒙.D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})>0\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad\text{rank}(\nabla d_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1}))=k\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x_{k+1}\not\in A_{\bm{x}}.

For the first equivalence, we used the fact that rank​(A​AT)=rank​(A)\text{rank}(AA^{T})=\text{rank}(A) for any matrix AA, and for the second equivalence, we used that xk+1∉A𝒙x_{k+1}\not\in A_{\bm{x}} means {xj−xk+1}1≤j≤k\{x_{j}-x_{k+1}\}_{1\leq j\leq k} is linearly independent. It follows that the set of critical points of d𝒙d_{\bm{x}} has dimension k−1k-1:

dim​{xk+1∈ℝn:D𝒙​(xk+1)=0}=dim​(A𝒙)=k−1\text{dim}\{x_{k+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})=0\}=\text{dim}(A_{\bm{x}})=k-1

and thus the set of critical values

C𝒙:=d𝒙​(A𝒙∖{x1,…,xk})C_{\bm{x}}:=d_{\bm{x}}(A_{\bm{x}}\setminus\{x_{1},...,x_{k}\})

has Lebesgue measure zero in (0,∞)k(0,\infty)^{k}. Therefore by the regular value theorem, d𝒙−1​(𝒕)=Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)d_{\bm{x}}^{-1}(\bm{t})=S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}) is an (n−k)(n-k)-dimensional sphere (or empty) for all 𝒕∉C𝒙\bm{t}\not\in C_{\bm{x}}.

Therefore

C𝒙={𝒕∈ℝk:Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)​ is a point}C_{\bm{x}}=\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})\text{ is a point}\}

Also let

Z𝒙={𝒕∈ℝk:Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)=∅}.Z_{\bm{x}}=\{\bm{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})=\emptyset\}.

We are now ready to define the spherical averaging operator.

Definition 2.4.

Let 𝒙∈Aff\bm{x}\in\textup{Aff}. We define

𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙):=∫Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)f⁡(y)​d​σ𝒙,𝒕​(y),𝒕∉C𝒙∪Z𝒙\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x}):=\int_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})}f(y)\,d\sigma_{\bm{x},\bm{t}}(y),\quad\bm{t}\not\in C_{\bm{x}}\cup Z_{\bm{x}}

and define 𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)=0\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})=0 for 𝒕∈C𝒙∪Z𝒙\bm{t}\in C_{\bm{x}}\cup Z_{\bm{x}}. Here the surface measure σ𝒙,𝒕\sigma_{\bm{x},\bm{t}} on Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}) is

d​σ𝒙,𝒕​(xk+1):=d​ℋn−k|Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)​(xk+1)D𝒙​(xk+1)d\sigma_{\bm{x},\bm{t}}(x_{k+1}):=\frac{d\mathcal{H}^{n-k}|_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})}(x_{k+1})}{D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})}

where ℋn−k|Sn−k\mathcal{H}^{n-k}|_{S^{n-k}} is the unnormalized (n−k)(n-k)-dimensional Hausdorff measure on Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}).

Remark 2.5.

If 𝒕∉C𝒙\bm{t}\not\in C_{\bm{x}} then by definition, 𝒕\bm{t} is a regular value of d𝒙d_{\bm{x}} and so for xk+1∈Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)x_{k+1}\in S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t}), we know that D𝒙​(xk+1)>0D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})>0. Therefore the definition of σ𝒙,𝒕\sigma_{\bm{x},\bm{t}} makes sense.

Remark 2.6.

The reason we choose this definition is so that we can identify the measure 𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)​d​𝒕\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})\,d\bm{t} with the pushforward of ff under the distance map d𝒙d_{\bm{x}}. Indeed, using the coarea formula, we can compute

∫ℝkg⁡(𝒕)​d​((d𝒙)∗​(f​d​xk+1))​(𝒕)\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}g(\bm{t})d((d_{\bm{x}})_{*}(f\,dx_{k+1}))(\bm{t}) =∫ℝng⁡(|xk+1−x1|,…,|xk+1−xk|)​f​(xk+1)​d​xk+1\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}g(|x_{k+1}-x_{1}|,...,|x_{k+1}-x_{k}|)f(x_{k+1})\,dx_{k+1}
=∫(0,∞)k∫Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)g⁡(𝒕)​f​(xk+1)​D𝒙​(xk+1)−1​d​ℋn−k​(xk+1)​𝑑𝒕\displaystyle=\int_{(0,\infty)^{k}}\int_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})}g(\bm{t})f(x_{k+1})D_{\bm{x}}(x_{k+1})^{-1}\,d\mathcal{H}^{n-k}(x_{k+1})\,d\bm{t}
=∫(0,∞)kg⁡(𝒕)​𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)​𝑑𝒕.\displaystyle=\int_{(0,\infty)^{k}}g(\bm{t})\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})\,d\bm{t}.

In particular, by setting g=1g=1, we obtain the generalized polar coordinates formula

∫ℝnf⁡(xk+1)​d​xk+1=∫(0,∞)k∫Sn−k​(𝒙,𝒕)f⁡(xk+1)​d​σ𝒙,𝒕​(xk+1)​𝑑𝒕.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x_{k+1})\,dx_{k+1}=\int_{(0,\infty)^{k}}\int_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\bm{t})}f(x_{k+1})\,d\sigma_{\bm{x},\bm{t}}(x_{k+1})\,d\bm{t}.

Also note that the pushforward measure (d𝒙)∗​(f)​(𝒕)(d_{\bm{x}})_{*}(f)(\bm{t}) and 𝒜𝒕​(f)​(𝒙)\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}(f)(\bm{x}) have the same support as measures in the variable 𝒕\bm{t}, contained in the kk-star set of interest.

Remark 2.7.

By setting k=1k=1, the definition of 𝒜\mathcal{A} gives the spherical average operator with respect to unnormalized surface measure:

𝒜t​f​(x)=∫Sn−1​(x,t)f⁡(y)​d​σx,t​(y).\mathcal{A}_{t}f(x)=\int_{S^{n-1}(x,t)}f(y)\,d\sigma_{x,t}(y).

In the literature, the spherical average operator is usually defined with the normalized surface measure, but we choose to define our operator to be unnormalized because it makes the coarea identity above more direct.

Next, for x∈ℝn∖{0}x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}, let Γx:(−1/4,∞)→(0,∞)\Gamma_{x}:(-1/4,\infty)\to(0,\infty) denote the map

Γx​(s)=|x|​1+4​s.\Gamma_{x}(s)=|x|\sqrt{1+4s}.

The importance of this map in our context comes from the fact observed in [17] that for a fixed point y∈ℙ∞n∖{0}y\in\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\infty}\setminus\{0\}, and s>−1/4s>-1/4, then for any x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

(2.1) y⋅(x,|x|2)=s⇔|π⁡(y)−x|=Γπ⁡(y)​(s).y\cdot(x,|x|^{2})=s\quad\Leftrightarrow|\pi(y)-x|=\Gamma_{\pi(y)}(s).

Checking the equivalence above is straightforward by squaring and unraveling definitions in the equality on the right-hand side. This equivalence carries rich geometric information. Indeed, for y∈ℙ∞ny\in\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\infty} consider the following level set of the map that takes the dot product between a point in the paraboloid and yy,

ℒy​(s):={(x,|x|2)∈ℙ∞n:y⋅(x,|x|2)=s},\mathcal{L}_{y}(s):=\{(x,|x|^{2})\in\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\infty}\colon y\cdot(x,|x|^{2})=s\},

which is the intersection of the paraboloid ℙ∞n\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\infty} with a hyperplane of normal direction yy. Identity (2.1) tell us if we orthogonally project ℒy​(s)\mathcal{L}_{y}(s) onto the first nn coordinates, we obtain a sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} centered at π⁡(y)=−y¯2​|y¯|2\pi(y)=\frac{-\bar{y}}{2|\bar{y}|^{2}} and radius Γπ⁡(y)​(s):=|π⁡(y)|​1+4​s\Gamma_{\pi(y)}(s):=|\pi(y)|\sqrt{1+4s}, that is, a level set of the map dπ⁡(y)​(x)=|x−π⁡(y)|d_{\pi(y)}(x)=|x-\pi(y)|. We illustrate that in Figure 2 with n=2n=2 and y=(0,−1,1)y=(0,-1,1), in which case π⁡(y)=(0,1/2)\pi(y)=(0,1/2).

Next, we will introduce some notation that will be useful for the next lemma. Define

Jx​(s):=Γx′​(s)=2​|x|1+4​s=2​|x|2Γx​(s).J_{x}(s):=\Gamma_{x}^{\prime}(s)=\frac{2|x|}{\sqrt{1+4s}}=\frac{2|x|^{2}}{\Gamma_{x}(s)}.

We also define for 𝒙∈ℝk​n\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{kn}, Γ𝒙:(−1/4,∞)k→(0,∞)k\Gamma_{\bm{x}}:(-1/4,\infty)^{k}\to(0,\infty)^{k} and J𝒙:(−1/4,∞)k→ℝJ_{\bm{x}}:(-1/4,\infty)^{k}\to\mathbb{R} as

Γ𝒙​(𝒔):=(Γx1​(s1),…,Γxk​(sk))\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s}):=\bigl(\Gamma_{x_{1}}(s_{1}),\dots,\Gamma_{x_{k}}(s_{k})\bigr)

and

J𝒙(𝒔):=Jx1(s1)⋯Jxk(sk).J_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s}):=J_{x_{1}}(s_{1})\cdots J_{x_{k}}(s_{k}).

Finally, for 𝒕∈(0,∞)k\bm{t}\in(0,\infty)^{k}, set

(2.2) W⁡(𝒙,𝒕):=∏j=1kJxj​(Γxj−1​(tj))=2k|x1|2⋯|xk|2t1⋯tk.W(\bm{x},\bm{t}):=\prod_{j=1}^{k}J_{x_{j}}(\Gamma_{x_{j}}^{-1}(t_{j}))=\frac{2^{k}|x_{1}|^{2}\cdots|x_{k}|^{2}}{t_{1}\cdots t_{k}}.

The following theorem relates the L2L^{2} integral of 𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x}) with respect to the weight WW to a weighted L2L^{2} integral of the Fourier extension operator ℰ​f\mathcal{E}f.

Lemma 2.8.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. For any 𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Aff\bm{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\in\textup{Aff}, with xi≠0x_{i}\neq 0 for all 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, define yj:=π−1​(xj)y_{j}:=\pi^{-1}(x_{j}) for all 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k. Then,

∫(0,∞)k|𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)|2​W​(𝒙,𝒕)​𝑑𝒕=∫ℝk|ℰ​f​(s1​y1+⋯+sk​yk)|2​𝑑𝒔,\int_{(0,\infty)^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})|^{2}W(\bm{x},\bm{t})\,d\bm{t}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}|\mathcal{E}f(s_{1}y_{1}+\cdots+s_{k}y_{k})|^{2}\,d\bm{s},

for any f∈C0∞​(Bn​(0,1))f\in C^{\infty}_{0}(B^{n}(0,1)), where W⁡(𝐱,𝐭)W(\bm{x},\bm{t}) is defined as in (2.2).

Remark 2.9.

Before proving this lemma, we note that for k=1k=1, it follows that

∫0∞|𝒜t​f​(x1)|2​W​(x1,t)​𝑑t=∫ℝ|ℰ​f​(s1​y1)|2​d​s1.\int_{0}^{\infty}|\mathcal{A}_{t}f(x_{1})|^{2}W(x_{1},t)\,dt=\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\mathcal{E}f(s_{1}y_{1})|^{2}\,ds_{1}.

We can compare this with Liu’s identity, which gives

∫0∞|σt∗f⁡(x1)|2​tn−1​𝑑t=∫0∞|σ^s1∗f⁡(x1)|2​s1n−1​d​s1=∫0∞|ℰs1​𝕊n−1​(fwidecheck)​(x1)|2​s1n−1​d​s1,\int_{0}^{\infty}|\sigma_{t}*f(x_{1})|^{2}t^{n-1}dt=\int_{0}^{\infty}|\widehat{\sigma}_{s_{1}}*f(x_{1})|^{2}{s_{1}}^{n-1}ds_{1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}|\mathcal{E}_{s_{1}\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}(\widecheck{f})(x_{1})|^{2}s_{1}^{n-1}ds_{1},

where ℰs1​𝕊n−1(g)(x)=∫g(w)e−2πix⋅wdσ~s1(w),\mathcal{E}_{s_{1}\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}(g)(x)=\int g(w)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot w}d\tilde{\sigma}_{s_{1}}(w), for σ~s1\tilde{\sigma}_{s_{1}} the normalized surface measure in the sphere of radius s1s_{1} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. We observe two key differences. One is that the extension operator in our identity is the extension operator associated to the truncated paraboloid ℙn⊂ℝn+1\mathbb{P}^{n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}, while Liu’s identity leads to an extension estimate for an (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional sphere in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Secondly, our extension operator is acting on ff, while in Liu’s identity the extension operator acts on fwidecheck\widecheck{f}.

Proof of Lemma 2.8.

The idea of the proof can essentially be summarized as: perform a change of variables, then apply Plancherel, then apply the reverse change of variables as before. With 𝒙=(x1,x2,…,xk)\bm{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k}) fixed, we compute

by making the change of variables sj=Γxj−1​(tj)s_{j}=\Gamma_{x_{j}}^{-1}(t_{j}).

𝒔↦𝒜Γ𝒙​(𝒔)f(𝒙)J𝒙(𝒔)1(−1/4,∞)k(𝒔)\bm{s}\mapsto\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})}f(\bm{x})J_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})1_{(-1/4,\infty)^{k}}(\bm{s})

and apply Plancherel. Indeed, for 𝝃∈ℝk\bm{\xi}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} we compute

(2.3) ∫(−1/4,∞)k𝒜Γ𝒙​(𝒔)f(𝒙)J𝒙(𝒔)e−2πi𝒔⋅𝝃d𝒔=∫(−1/4,∞)k∫Sn−k​(𝒙,Γ𝒙​(𝒔))f(xk+1)J𝒙(𝒔)e−2πi𝝃⋅𝒔dσ𝒙,Γ𝒙​(𝒔)(xk+1)d𝒔.\begin{split}&\int_{(-1/4,\infty)^{k}}\mathcal{A}_{\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})}f(\bm{x})J_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})e^{-2\pi i\bm{s}\cdot\bm{\xi}}\,d\bm{s}\\ &=\int_{(-1/4,\infty)^{k}}\int_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s}))}f(x_{k+1})J_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})e^{-2\pi i\bm{\xi}\cdot\bm{s}}\,d\sigma_{\bm{x},\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})}(x_{k+1})\,d\bm{s}.\end{split}

|xj−xk+1|=Γxj(sj)⇔yj⋅(xk+1,|xk+1|2)=sj|x_{j}-x_{k+1}|=\Gamma_{x_{j}}(s_{j})\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad y_{j}\cdot(x_{k+1},|x_{k+1}|^{2})=s_{j}

where yj=π−1​(xj)y_{j}=\pi^{-1}(x_{j}).

So by substituting this expression for sjs_{j} in (2.3),

=∫(−1/4,∞)k∫Sn−k​(𝒙,Γ𝒙​(𝒔))f(xk+1)J𝒙(𝒔)e−2πi(ξ1y1+⋯+ξkyk)⋅(xk+1,|xk+1|2)dσ𝒙,Γ𝒙​(𝒔)(xk+1)d𝒔.\displaystyle=\int_{(-1/4,\infty)^{k}}\int_{S^{n-k}(\bm{x},\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s}))}f(x_{k+1})J_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})e^{-2\pi i(\xi_{1}y_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{k}y_{k})\cdot(x_{k+1},|x_{k+1}|^{2})}\,d\sigma_{\bm{x},\Gamma_{\bm{x}}(\bm{s})}(x_{k+1})\,d\bm{s}.

Averaging the identity in Lemma 2.8 over the pins leads to a global weighted extension estimate, where the weight is explicitly described as a convolution of measures supported on families of lines determined by the pinned sets. That is precisely described in the theorem below.

Theorem 2.10.

Assume n≥2n\geq 2 and 1≤k<n1\leq k<n. Let μ1,…,μk\mu_{1},...,\mu_{k} be finite compactly supported Borel measures on ℝn∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\} and let 𝛍:=μ1×⋯×μk\bm{\mu}:=\mu_{1}\times\cdots\times\mu_{k}. Suppose that 𝛍⁡((Aff)c)=0\bm{\mu}((\textup{Aff})^{c})=0. Then for any f∈C0∞​(Bn​(0,1))f\in C^{\infty}_{0}(B^{n}(0,1)),

∫∫(0,∞)k|𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)|2​W​(𝒙,𝒕)​𝑑𝒕​𝑑𝝁​(𝒙)=∫ℝn+1|ℰ​f​(y)|2​𝑑w​(y)\int\int_{(0,\infty)^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})|^{2}W(\bm{x},\bm{t})\,d\bm{t}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}dw(y)

where w=wk,μ1,…,μkw=w_{k,\mu_{1},...,\mu_{k}} is the measure defined by the kk-fold convolution

w=w1∗⋯∗wkw=w_{1}*\cdots*w_{k}

and wj:=Φ∗​(μj×d​t)w_{j}:=\Phi_{*}(\mu_{j}\times dt), and the map Φ:(ℝn∖{0})×(ℝ∖{0})→(ℝn∖{0})×(ℝ∖{0})\Phi:(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\})\times(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})\to(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\})\times(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}) is defined by

In the applications of this theorem later, the measures μj\mu_{j} will be Frostman measures restricted to subsets of EE from which the pins are chosen. Remark 2.11.

3. Facts About the Weights

In this section, we will study the weight ww defined in Theorem 2.10. We will now specialize to the case where μ1,…,μk\mu_{1},...,\mu_{k} are α\alpha-Frostman measures satisfying the support condition

supp​μj⊂{x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}\text{supp}\,\mu_{j}\subset\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\}

as well as the transversality condition:

(3.1) |x1∧⋯∧xk|≳1,for all ​xj∈Ej:=supp​μj.|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\gtrsim 1,\quad\text{for all }x_{j}\in E_{j}:=\text{supp}\,\mu_{j}.

Thus (3.1) is a quantitative linear independence condition on the sets E1,…,EkE_{1},\dots,E_{k}. When dealing with distance graphs in E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, we can usually reduce to this scenario due to Lemma 4.2. Note that the condition above implies in particular 𝝁⁡((Aff)c)=0\bm{\mu}((\text{Aff})^{c})=0.

The measures wjw_{j} obtained in this case can be seen as a (n+1)(n+1)-dimensional extension of the α\alpha-Frostman measures μj\mu_{j}. We will indeed show in particular that the measures wjw_{j} and ww can be decomposed into a sum of (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measures.

We fix dyadic scales R0,R1,R2,⋯R_{0},R_{1},R_{2},\cdots where Ri=2iR_{i}=2^{i}. Let ARA_{R} denote the annulus

AR:={y∈ℝn+1:R/2≤|y|≤R}A_{R}:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:R/2\leq|y|\leq R\}

and let B0B_{0} denote the unit ball

B0:={y∈ℝn+1:|y|≤1}.B_{0}:=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:|y|\leq 1\}.
Theorem 3.1.

Let μ1,…,μk\mu_{1},...,\mu_{k} be α\alpha-Frostman measures satisfying the support condition

supp​μj⊂{x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}\text{supp}\,\mu_{j}\subset\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\}

and 3.1 and let wjw_{j}, ww be the measures defined in Theorem 2.10. I.e.,

wj=Φ∗(μj×dt),w=w1∗⋯∗wk,Φ(x,t)=t4​|x|2(−2x,1).w_{j}=\Phi_{*}(\mu_{j}\times dt),\quad w=w_{1}*\cdots*w_{k},\quad\Phi(x,t)=\frac{t}{4|x|^{2}}(-2x,1).

Let w0w^{0} be the restriction of ww to B0B_{0} and for each i≥1i\geq 1, let wiw^{i} denote the restriction of ww to ARiA_{R_{i}} rescaled by Riα−k+1R_{i}^{\alpha-k+1}. I.e.

w0:=w|B0,wi:=Riα−k+1​w|ARi.w^{0}:=w|_{B_{0}},\quad w^{i}:=R_{i}^{\alpha-k+1}w|_{A_{R_{i}}}.

Then w0​(B0)≲1w^{0}(B_{0})\lesssim 1 and wiw^{i} is an (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measure on Bn+1​(0,Ri)B^{n+1}(0,R_{i}). In other words, we have a decomposition of ww into a sum of (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measures:

w=w0+∑i=1∞Ri−α+k−1​wi.w=w^{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1}w^{i}.

Before proving the theorem above, we will need a few lemmas. For the remainder of this section, we will fix μ1,⋯,μk\mu_{1},\cdots,\mu_{k} and w,wiw,w^{i} as in the statement of the theorem. We also define for each 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k the measures wjiw_{j}^{i} from wjw_{j} analogously to wiw^{i}:

(3.2) wj0:=wj|B0,wji:=Riα​wj|ARi.w_{j}^{0}:=w_{j}|_{B_{0}},\quad w_{j}^{i}:=R_{i}^{\alpha}w_{j}|_{A_{R_{i}}}.

wj=wj0+∑i=1∞Ri−α​wji.w_{j}=w_{j}^{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}R_{i}^{-\alpha}w_{j}^{i}.

We start by stating a simple lemma about the support of the measures wjw_{j}. Observe that

Φ−1​(x,t)=1t​(−x2,|x|2).\Phi^{-1}(x,t)=\frac{1}{t}\left(-\frac{x}{2},|x|^{2}\right).

Lemma 3.2.

Let Sj:=supp​wjS_{j}:=\text{supp}\,w_{j}. Then Sj⊂{y=(x,t)∈ℝn+1:|x|≈|t|}S_{j}\subset\{y=(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:|x|\approx|t|\}.

Proof.

{x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}×ℝ.\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\}\times\mathbb{R}.

Φ⁡({x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}×ℝ).\Phi\left(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\}\times\mathbb{R}\right).

|φ1​(y)−φ1​(y′)|≲R−1​|y−y′|,|φ2​(y)−φ2​(y′)|≲|y−y′|.|\varphi_{1}(y)-\varphi_{1}(y^{\prime})|\lesssim R^{-1}|y-y^{\prime}|,\quad|\varphi_{2}(y)-\varphi_{2}(y^{\prime})|\lesssim|y-y^{\prime}|.

We omit the proof of this lemma since it is a straightforward computation.

Lemma 3.4.

For all R≥1R\geq 1, we have that wj​(Bn+1​(0,R))≲Rw_{j}(B^{n+1}(0,R))\lesssim R and for each i≥1i\geq 1, the weight wjiw_{j}^{i} defined in equation (3.2) is an (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measure on Bn+1​(0,Ri)B^{n+1}(0,R_{i}). wji​(Bn+1​(y,r))=Riα​wj​(Bn+1​(y,r)∩ARi)≲rα+1,w_{j}^{i}(B^{n+1}(y,r))=R_{i}^{\alpha}w_{j}(B^{n+1}(y,r)\cap A_{R_{i}})\lesssim r^{\alpha+1},

as wanted. ∎

It follows from the hypothesis on EjE_{j} that they are separated and linearly independent in the sense that if xj∈Ejx_{j}\in E_{j} for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, then {xj}j=1k\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{k} is linearly independent. Define Cj=ρ⁡(Sj∖{0})C_{j}=\rho(S_{j}\setminus\{0\}), where ρ\rho denotes the radial projection map defined by

ρ:ℝn+1∖{0}→𝕊n,ρ⁡(y)=y|y|.\rho:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{S}^{n},\quad\rho(y)=\frac{y}{|y|}.

zj=±(−2​xj,1)4​|xj|2+1,xj∈Ej.z_{j}=\pm\frac{(-2x_{j},1)}{\sqrt{4|x_{j}|^{2}+1}},\qquad x_{j}\in E_{j}.

Since ww is a convolution of the wjw_{j}, it is important to establish some transversality properties of the supports of the wjw_{j}.

Lemma 3.5.

For yj∈Sj=supp​wjy_{j}\in S_{j}=\textup{supp}\,w_{j}, we have

Let

A:={a∈ℝk:∑j=1k|aj|=1}.A:=\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:\sum_{j=1}^{k}|a_{j}|=1\right\}.

C1×⋯×Ck×A→ℝn+1,(z1,…,zk,a)↦a1z1+⋯+akzkC_{1}\times\cdots\times C_{k}\times A\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1},\qquad(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k},a)\mapsto a_{1}z_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}z_{k}

|a1z1+⋯+akzk|≳1, for all (z1,…,zk,a)∈C1×⋯×Ck×A.|a_{1}z_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}z_{k}|\gtrsim 1,\quad\text{ for all }(z_{1},\ldots,z_{k},a)\in C_{1}\times\cdots\times C_{k}\times A.

y1+⋯+yk=(|y1|+⋯+|yk|)​(a1​z1+⋯+ak​zk).y_{1}+\cdots+y_{k}=(|y_{1}|+\cdots+|y_{k}|)(a_{1}z_{1}+\cdots+a_{k}z_{k}).

|y1+⋯+yk|≳|y1|+⋯+|yk|,|y_{1}+\cdots+y_{k}|\gtrsim|y_{1}|+\cdots+|y_{k}|,

We are now ready to prove Theorem 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

The case k=1k=1 follows directly from Lemma 3.4, so assume k≥2k\geq 2.

We first prove the estimate on B0B_{0}. If yj∈Sjy_{j}\in S_{j} and y1+⋯+yk∈B0y_{1}+\cdots+y_{k}\in B_{0}, then Lemma 3.5 gives

|y1|+⋯+|yk|≲|y1+⋯+yk|≲R,|y_{1}|+\cdots+|y_{k}|\lesssim|y_{1}+\cdots+y_{k}|\lesssim R,

while the reverse inequality

R≲|y1+⋯+yk|≤|y1|+⋯+|yk|R\lesssim|y_{1}+\cdots+y_{k}|\leq|y_{1}|+\cdots+|y_{k}|

4. Weighted Fourier Extension Estimates

In this section, we prove Theorem A. To summarize, we use the results of the previous section to reduce the proof of Theorem A to a local weighted Fourier extension estimate involving the weight ww. We can then apply known weighted restriction estimates to prove Theorem A.

For any R>0R>0, let 𝒫≤R\mathcal{P}_{\leq R} and 𝒫≥R\mathcal{P}_{\geq R} denote the Littlewood-Paley projections onto frequencies {|ξ|≤R}\{|\xi|\leq R\} and {|ξ|≥R}\{|\xi|\geq R\} respectively. We start by stating an elementary lemma.

Lemma 4.1.

Let R≥1R\geq 1 and ff be a function with support in the unit ball of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then for any s,N>0s,N>0

sup|y|≤R|ℰ(𝒫≥4​Rf)(y)|≲s,NR−N∥f∥H−s.\sup_{|y|\leq R}|\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}_{\geq 4R}f)(y)|\lesssim_{s,N}R^{-N}\|f\|_{H^{-s}}.
Proof.

The proof is fairly standard but we include a sketch for completeness. Let y=(x,t)y=(x,t) with |y|≤R|y|\leq R and consider the function

ay​(z)=χ⁡(z)​e2​π​i​(x⋅z+t​|z|2)a_{y}(z)=\chi(z)e^{2\pi i(x\cdot z+t|z|^{2})}

where χ\chi is a smooth bump function equal to 11 on Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1) and supported on Bn​(0,5/4)B^{n}(0,5/4). Then

|ℰ​(𝒫≥4​R​f)​(y)|\displaystyle|\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{P}_{\geq 4R}f)(y)| =|∫ay​(z)​𝒫≥4​R​f​(z)​𝑑z|\displaystyle=\left|\int a_{y}(z)\mathcal{P}_{\geq 4R}f(z)\,dz\right|
=|∫|ξ|≥4​Ray^​(ξ)​f^​(ξ)​𝑑ξ|\displaystyle=\left|\int_{|\xi|\geq 4R}\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)\widehat{f}(\xi)\,d\xi\right|
≤‖f‖H−s​(∫|ξ|≥4​R⟨ξ⟩2​s​|ay^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ)1/2.\displaystyle\leq\|f\|_{H^{-s}}\left(\int_{|\xi|\geq 4R}\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}|\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi\right)^{1/2}.

The claim will follow once we show that

∫|ξ|≥4​R⟨ξ⟩2​s|ay^(ξ)|2dξ≲s,NR−2​N.\int_{|\xi|\geq 4R}\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}|\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi\lesssim_{s,N}R^{-2N}.

We can assume R≥1R\geq 1 (in the case R<1R<1 we use ∥ay∥Hs≲s1\|a_{y}\|_{H^{s}}\lesssim_{s}1). We write

ay^​(ξ)=∫χ⁡(z)​ei​Φy,ξ​(z)​𝑑z\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)=\int\chi(z)e^{i\Phi_{y,\xi}(z)}\,dz

where Φy,ξ​(z)=2​π​(x⋅z+t​|z|2−z⋅ξ)\Phi_{y,\xi}(z)=2\pi(x\cdot z+t|z|^{2}-z\cdot\xi). Since |z|≤5/4|z|\leq 5/4, |y|≤R|y|\leq R and |ξ|≥4​R|\xi|\geq 4R, we have that

|∇zΦy,ξ​(z)|≳|ξ|.|\nabla_{z}\Phi_{y,\xi}(z)|\gtrsim|\xi|.

Applying integration by parts MM times, we have that

|ay^(ξ)|≲M|ξ|−M.|\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)|\lesssim_{M}|\xi|^{-M}.

Therefore

∫|ξ|≥4​R⟨ξ⟩2​s|ay^(ξ)|2dξ≲M∫|ξ|≥4​R|ξ|2​s−2​Mdξ≲s,NR−2​N\int_{|\xi|\geq 4R}\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}|\widehat{a_{y}}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi\lesssim_{M}\int_{|\xi|\geq 4R}|\xi|^{2s-2M}\,d\xi\lesssim_{s,N}R^{-2N}

by choosing MM sufficiently large depending on ss and NN. ∎

Lemma 4.2 (Transversality Lemma).

Let 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n and let E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} be a compact set. Let μ\mu be a nonzero ss-Frostman measure supported on EE, and assume s∈(k−1,n]s\in(k-1,n]. Let F1,…,Fk⊂supp​(μ)F_{1},\dots,F_{k}\subset\text{supp}(\mu) be μ\mu-measurable pairwise disjoint sets with μ⁡(Fi)>0\mu(F_{i})>0 for each ii.

Then there exist compact sets Ei⊂FiE_{i}\subset F_{i}, i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k, with μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0, and a constant c>0c>0, such that

|x1∧⋯∧xk|≥cfor all ​xi∈Ei.|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\geq c\qquad\text{for all }x_{i}\in E_{i}.
Remark 4.3.

In the [1] machinery for kk admissible graphs, it suffices to have the L2L^{2} kk-star building blocks for pins coming from transverse pieces. The reason is that any sufficient threshold α+∗​(n,k)∈(0,n)\alpha_{+}^{*}(n,k)\in(0,n) valid for positive measure of kk stars is at least kk by [1, Remark 7] (so larger than k−1k-1). Given a compact set EE of dimension larger than α+∗​(n,k)\alpha_{+}^{*}(n,k), one takes a Frostman measure μ\mu in EE with parameter s>α+∗​(n,k)s>\alpha_{+}^{*}(n,k) and find separated μ\mu positive measure compact pieces F1,F2,…,F|𝒱|⊂EF_{1},F_{2},\dots,F_{|\mathcal{V}|}\subset E where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the vertex set of the kk admissible graph we care for. Then one can successfully apply the lemma above to every kk out of |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| pieces. This only requires finitely many refining steps ((|𝒱|k)\binom{|\mathcal{V}|}{k} many steps) until we are reduced to pairwise disjoint compact pieces {Ei:1≤i≤|𝒱|}\{E_{i}\colon 1\leq i\leq|\mathcal{V}|\} such that μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0 for all ii, and such that any kk pieces {Eij}j=1k\{E_{i_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{k}, 1≤i1<i2<⋯<ik≤|𝒱|1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\dots<i_{k}\leq|\mathcal{V}| are transverse.

Proof of Lemma 4.2.

We first record a simple consequence of the Frostman condition. If VV is any linear subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with dimV≤k−1\dim V\leq k-1, then

μ⁡(V)=0.\mu(V)=0.

Indeed, since supp​(μ)\text{supp}(\mu) is compact, V∩supp​(μ)V\cap\text{supp}(\mu) can be covered by O(r−dimV)O(r^{-\dim V}) balls of radius rr. Hence, by the ss-Frostman condition, μ⁡(V)≲rs−dimV.\mu(V)\lesssim r^{s-\dim V}. Since s>k−1≥dimVs>k-1\geq\dim V, letting r→0r\to 0 gives μ⁡(V)=0\mu(V)=0.

Now define μi:=μFi\mu_{i}:=\mu_{F_{i}} (restriction of μ\mu to FiF_{i}). We claim that

(μ1×⋯×μk)({(x1,…,xk):x1∧⋯∧xk=0})=0.(\mu_{1}\times\cdots\times\mu_{k})\Bigl(\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}):x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}=0\}\Bigr)=0.

Equivalently, the set of linearly dependent kk-tuples has zero μ1×⋯×μk\mu_{1}\times\cdots\times\mu_{k}-measure.

We prove this by induction. For 1≤m≤k1\leq m\leq k, let

Zm:={(x1,…,xm):x1,…,xm are linearly dependent}.Z_{m}:=\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}):x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\text{ are linearly dependent}\}.

For m=1m=1, Z1={0}Z_{1}=\{0\}, and μ1​({0})=0\mu_{1}(\{0\})=0 by the observation above.

Assume the claim has been proved for m−1m-1. Then

Zm⊂(Zm−1×ℝn)∪{(x1,…,xm):x1,…,xm−1 are independent and xm∈span(x1,…,xm−1)}.Z_{m}\subset(Z_{m-1}\times\mathbb{R}^{n})\cup\{(x_{1},\dots,x_{m}):x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1}\text{ are independent and }x_{m}\in\text{span}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})\}.

The first set has zero product measure by the induction hypothesis. For the second set, fix an independent (m−1)(m-1)-tuple (x1,…,xm−1)(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1}). Then

span​(x1,…,xm−1)\text{span}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})

is an (m−1)(m-1)-dimensional linear subspace. Since m−1≤k−1m-1\leq k-1, the preliminary observation gives

μm​(span​(x1,…,xm−1))=0.\mu_{m}\bigl(\text{span}(x_{1},\dots,x_{m-1})\bigr)=0.

Fubini therefore gives that the second set also has zero product measure. This proves the claim for mm, and hence for m=km=k.

Since each μi\mu_{i} is nonzero, the product measure μ1×⋯×μk\mu_{1}\times\cdots\times\mu_{k} has positive total mass. Therefore we may choose

(a1,…,ak)∈F1×⋯×Fk(a_{1},\dots,a_{k})\in F_{1}\times\cdots\times F_{k}

outside the exceptional set, with each ai∈supp​(μi)a_{i}\in\text{supp}(\mu_{i}). Thus

|a1∧⋯∧ak|>0.|a_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge a_{k}|>0.

By continuity of the map

(x1,…,xk)↦|x1∧⋯∧xk|,(x_{1},\dots,x_{k})\mapsto|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|,

there exist radii ρi>0\rho_{i}>0 and a constant c>0c>0 such that

|x1∧⋯∧xk|≥c|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\geq c

whenever xi∈B⁡(ai,ρi)x_{i}\in B(a_{i},\rho_{i}) for every ii.

Since ai∈supp​(μi)a_{i}\in\text{supp}(\mu_{i}), we have

μi​(B⁡(ai,ρi))>0.\mu_{i}(B(a_{i},\rho_{i}))>0.

Equivalently,

μ⁡(Fi∩B⁡(ai,ρi))>0.\mu(F_{i}\cap B(a_{i},\rho_{i}))>0.

By inner regularity, choose compact sets

Ei⊂Fi∩B⁡(ai,ρi)E_{i}\subset F_{i}\cap B(a_{i},\rho_{i})

with μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0. Then, for all xi∈Eix_{i}\in E_{i},

|x1∧⋯∧xk|≥c.|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\geq c.

∎

Theorem 4.4.

Let α>0\alpha>0. Suppose that for some γ=γ⁡(α)≥0\gamma=\gamma(\alpha)\geq 0, we have the estimate

∫Bn+1​(0,R)|ℰ​f​(y)|2​𝑑ν​(y)≲Rγ​‖f‖L22\int_{B^{n+1}(0,R)}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}\,d\nu(y)\lesssim R^{\gamma}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

for all (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measures ν\nu in ℝn+1\mathbb{R}^{n+1} and ff supported on the unit ball in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Then if E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is a compact set with Hausdorff dimension

dim(E)>α>n+k−1+γ2,\dim(E)>\alpha>\frac{n+k-1+\gamma}{2},

and μ\mu is an α\alpha-Frostman measure on EE, then EE has an abundance of L2L^{2} kk-pinned stars relative to μ\mu and in particular, for an abundance of pins (x1,x2,…,xk)∈Ek(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{k})\in E^{k}, one has that

ℒk​(Δx1,…,xkk​-star​(E))>0.\mathcal{L}^{k}\bigl(\Delta_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}^{k\text{-star}}(E)\bigr)>0.
Proof.

Let μ\mu be an α\alpha-Frostman measure on EE. Let E1,…,Ek+1⊂E∖{0}E_{1},\dots,E_{k+1}\subset E\setminus\{0\} be a collection of k+1k+1 separated compact subsets of E∖{0}E\setminus\{0\} with μ⁡(Ei)>0\mu(E_{i})>0 for each 1≤i≤k+11\leq i\leq k+1 and {E1,E2,…,Ek}\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{k}\} transverse. More precisely, we are assuming the following properties

  1. (1)

    Positive measure: μ⁡(Ej)>0\mu(E_{j})>0 for each 1≤j≤k+11\leq j\leq k+1.

  2. (2)

    Transversality: |x1∧⋯∧xk|≳1|x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge x_{k}|\gtrsim 1 for all xj∈Ejx_{j}\in E_{j}, 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k.

  3. (3)

    Distance from the origin: For all 1≤j≤k+11\leq j\leq k+1 Ej⊂{x∈ℝn:ϵ≤|x|≤C}E_{j}\subset\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\epsilon\leq|x|\leq C\} where ϵ,C>0\epsilon,C>0. Up to a rescaling argument we can assume that ϵ=1/2\epsilon=1/2 and C=1C=1, so that Ej⊂{x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}E_{j}\subset\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\}.

In practice, collections of k+1k+1 pieces with these properties always exist whenever dim(E)>k−1\dim(E)>k-1. One first applies the standard separation Lemma in [4, Lemma 3] successively to get to disjoint k+1k+1 compact pieces of positive measure and that do not intersect the origin (properties (2) and (3)), and then for the transversality property, one applies the transversality Lemma to these pieces 4.2 (observe that it is relevant that α>n+k−12>k−1\alpha>\frac{n+k-1}{2}>k-1 so that Lemma applies).

For each 1≤j≤k+11\leq j\leq k+1, let μj\mu_{j} be corresponding α\alpha-Frostman measures on EjE_{j}, that is, μj=μEj\mu_{j}=\mu_{E_{j}}. As before denote 𝝁=∏j=1kμj\bm{\mu}=\prod_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{j}. It suffices to show that

(4.1) ∫∫ℝk|𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)|2​𝑑𝒕​𝑑𝝁​(𝒙)≲∫ℝn|ξ|−β​|f^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\int\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})|^{2}\,d\bm{t}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\xi|^{-\beta}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi

for all smooth compactly supported functions ff and some β>n−α\beta>n-\alpha. Indeed, if this is the case we set (μk+1)R=(μk+1)∗ηR(\mu_{k+1})_{R}=(\mu_{k+1})*\eta_{R} where

ηR​(x)=Rn​η​(R​x)\eta_{R}(x)=R^{n}\eta(Rx)

for some smooth compactly supported function η\eta with ∫η=1\int\eta=1. Then by (4.1), we have that

∫∫ℝk|𝒜𝒕​(μk+1)R​(𝒙)|2​𝑑𝒕​𝑑𝝁​(𝒙)≲∫ℝn|ξ|−β​|μk+1^​(ξ)|2​|η^​(R​ξ)|2​𝑑ξ≤∫ℝn|ξ|−β​|μk+1^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ<∞\int\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}(\mu_{k+1})_{R}(\bm{x})|^{2}\,d\bm{t}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\xi|^{-\beta}|\widehat{\mu_{k+1}}(\xi)|^{2}|\widehat{\eta}(R\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\xi|^{-\beta}|\widehat{\mu_{k+1}}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi<\infty

since β>n−α\beta>n-\alpha and μk+1\mu_{k+1} is α\alpha-Frostman. Passing to the limit as R→∞R\to\infty, we obtain

∫E1×⋯×Ek∥(d𝒙)∗μk+1∥L2​(ℝk)2d𝝁(𝒙)<∞.\int_{E_{1}\times\cdots\times E_{k}}\|(d_{\bm{x}})_{*}\mu_{k+1}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{k})}^{2}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})<\infty.

Hence

(d𝒙)∗​μk+1∈L2​(ℝk)(d_{\bm{x}})_{*}\mu_{k+1}\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{k})

for 𝝁\bm{\mu}-almost every 𝒙∈E1×⋯×Ek\bm{x}\in E_{1}\times\cdots\times E_{k}, which is the conclusion of the theorem.

It remains to establish (4.1). By Theorem 2.10, for all smooth and compactly supported functions ff, we have that

∫∫ℝk|𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)|2​W​(𝒙,𝒕)​𝑑𝒕​𝑑𝝁​(𝒙)=∫ℝn+1|ℰ​f​(y)|2​𝑑w​(y)\int\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})|^{2}W(\bm{x},\bm{t})\,d\bm{t}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}dw(y)

where the weight ww is defined in Theorem 2.10. Using the compact support of ff and the μj\mu_{j},

𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)=0\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})=0

if tj≥Ct_{j}\geq C for some tjt_{j}. Therefore we have that

W⁡(𝒙,𝒕)=2k|x1|2⋯|xk|2t1⋯tk≳1W(\bm{x},\bm{t})=\frac{2^{k}|x_{1}|^{2}\cdots|x_{k}|^{2}}{t_{1}\cdots t_{k}}\gtrsim 1

in the integration region. In particular,

∫∫ℝk|𝒜𝒕​f​(𝒙)|2​𝑑𝒕​𝑑𝝁​(𝒙)≲∫ℝn+1|ℰ​f​(y)|2​𝑑w​(y).\int\int_{\mathbb{R}^{k}}|\mathcal{A}_{\bm{t}}f(\bm{x})|^{2}\,d\bm{t}\,d\bm{\mu}(\bm{x})\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}dw(y).

By Theorem 3.1, we can write

w=w0+∑i=1∞Ri−α+k−1​wiw=w^{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1}w^{i}

where w0​(B0)≲1w^{0}(B_{0})\lesssim 1 and each wiw^{i} is an (α+1)(\alpha+1)-Frostman measure on Bn+1​(0,Ri)B^{n+1}(0,R_{i}). Therefore we can write

∫ℝn+1|ℰ​f​(y)|2​𝑑w​(y)≲∫B0|ℰ​f​(y)|2​d​w0​(y)+∑i=1∞Ri−α+k−1​∫ARi|ℰ​f​(y)|2​d​wi​(y).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}\,dw(y)\lesssim\int_{B_{0}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}\,dw^{0}(y)+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1}\int_{A_{R_{i}}}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}\,dw^{i}(y).

Let f≤R:=𝒫≤R​ff_{\leq R}:=\mathcal{P}_{\leq R}f and f≥R:=𝒫≥R​ff_{\geq R}:=\mathcal{P}_{\geq R}f. By Lemma 4.1, we have that

|ℰf(y)−ℰf≤4​R(y)|≲s,NR−N∥f∥H−s|\mathcal{E}f(y)-\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4R}(y)|\lesssim_{s,N}R^{-N}\|f\|_{H^{-s}}

for all y∈Bn+1​(0,R)y\in B^{n+1}(0,R) and any s,N>0s,N>0. Therefore if NN is large enough, the right hand side is bounded by a constant times

∫B0|ℰ​f≤4​(y)|2​d​w0​(y)+∑i=1∞Ri−α+k−1​∫ARi|ℰ​f≤4​Ri​(y)|2​d​wi​(y)+‖f‖H−s2.\int_{B_{0}}|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4}(y)|^{2}\,dw^{0}(y)+\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1}\int_{A_{R_{i}}}|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4R_{i}}(y)|^{2}\,dw^{i}(y)+\|f\|_{H^{-s}}^{2}.

To bound the first term, we can simply use

∫B0|ℰ​f≤4​(y)|2​d​w0​(y)\displaystyle\int_{B_{0}}|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4}(y)|^{2}\,dw^{0}(y) ≤‖ℰ​f≤4‖L∞​(B0)2​w0​(B0)\displaystyle\leq\|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4}\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{0})}^{2}w^{0}(B_{0})
≲‖ℰ​f≤4‖L∞​(B0)2\displaystyle\lesssim\|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4}\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{0})}^{2}

∫ARi|ℰ​f≤4​Ri​(y)|2​d​wi​(y)≲Riγ​‖f≤4​Ri‖L22.\int_{A_{R_{i}}}|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4R_{i}}(y)|^{2}\,dw^{i}(y)\lesssim R_{i}^{\gamma}\|f_{\leq 4R_{i}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.

By the assumption on α\alpha, there is some small ϵ>0\epsilon>0 so that

β:=α−k+1−γ−ϵ>n−α.\beta:=\alpha-k+1-\gamma-\epsilon>n-\alpha.

Therefore

Ri−α+k−1​∫ARi|ℰ​f≤4​Ri​(y)|2​d​wi​(y)\displaystyle R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1}\int_{A_{R_{i}}}|\mathcal{E}f_{\leq 4R_{i}}(y)|^{2}\,dw^{i}(y) ≲Ri−ϵ​Ri−α+k−1+γ+ϵ​‖f≤4​Ri‖L22\displaystyle\lesssim R_{i}^{-\epsilon}R_{i}^{-\alpha+k-1+\gamma+\epsilon}\|f_{\leq 4R_{i}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}
≤Ri−ϵ​Ri−β​∫|ξ|≤4​Ri|f^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\displaystyle\leq R_{i}^{-\epsilon}R_{i}^{-\beta}\int_{|\xi|\leq 4R_{i}}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi
≲Ri−ϵ​∫|ξ|≤4​Ri|f^​(ξ)|2​|ξ|−β​𝑑ξ.\displaystyle\lesssim R_{i}^{-\epsilon}\int_{|\xi|\leq 4R_{i}}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}|\xi|^{-\beta}\,d\xi.

By choosing ss large enough so that 2​s>β2s>\beta, we conclude (4.1) as wanted. ∎

Theorem A is now a simple consequence of the theorem above and the local weighted Fourier extension estimate established in [6].

Theorem 4.5 (Du–Zhang).

Let ν\nu be an η\eta-Frostman measure on Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R). For all ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we have the estimate

∫Bn+1​(0,R)|ℰf(y)|2dν(y)≲ϵRηn+1+ϵ∥f∥L22.\int_{B^{n+1}(0,R)}|\mathcal{E}f(y)|^{2}\,d\nu(y)\lesssim_{\epsilon}R^{\frac{\eta}{n+1}+\epsilon}\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}.
Proof of Theorem A.

By Theorem 4.5, applied with η=α+1\eta=\alpha+1, the hypothesis of Theorem 4.4 is satisfied with

γ=α+1n+1+ϵ\gamma=\frac{\alpha+1}{n+1}+\epsilon

for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Since

α>α+​(n,k)=n2+k​n+k2​n+1,\alpha>\alpha_{+}(n,k)=\frac{n^{2}+kn+k}{2n+1},

we have

2​α>n+k−1+α+1n+1.2\alpha>n+k-1+\frac{\alpha+1}{n+1}.

Choosing ϵ>0\epsilon>0 sufficiently small, we obtain

2​α>n+k−1+α+1n+1+ϵ=n+k−1+γ.2\alpha>n+k-1+\frac{\alpha+1}{n+1}+\epsilon=n+k-1+\gamma.

Equivalently,

α>n+k−1+γ2.\alpha>\frac{n+k-1+\gamma}{2}.

Therefore the assumptions of Theorem 4.4 are satisfied, and hence EE has an abundance of L2L^{2} kk-pinned stars relative to μ\mu. ∎

As a consequence of Theorem 2.10 as well as Liu’s identity, we can derive a relationship between the Fourier extension operator for the paraboloid and the Fourier extension operator for the sphere. Indeed, let μ\mu be a measure supported on the annulus {x∈ℝn:1/2≤|x|≤1}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:1/2\leq|x|\leq 1\} and let ff be a function supported on the unit ball with support positive distance from supp​μ\text{supp}\,\mu. Then by Theorem 2.10, for k=1k=1, we have

∫ℝn∫ℝ|𝒜t​f​(x)|2​2​|x|2t​𝑑t​𝑑μ​(x)=∫ℝn+1|ℰℙn​f​(y)|2​𝑑w​(y)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}|\mathcal{A}_{t}f(x)|^{2}\frac{2|x|^{2}}{t}\,dt\,d\mu(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n+1}}|\mathcal{E}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}f(y)|^{2}dw(y)

where

w=Φ∗​(μ×d​t),Φ⁡(x,t)=t4​|x|2​(−2​x,1).w=\Phi_{*}(\mu\times dt),\quad\Phi(x,t)=\frac{t}{4|x|^{2}}(-2x,1).

Since the supports of μ\mu and ff are at positive distance from one another, we have that t≈1t\approx 1 for all tt in the integration region. Letting

relating the Fourier extension operator for the paraboloid to the Fourier extension operator for the sphere. Now assume that μ\mu is α\alpha-Frostman. In the proof of Theorem 4.4 for k=1k=1, we showed that

for the existence of pinned distance sets with positive measure. However, if one uses Du-Zhang’s weighted restriction estimates for the (n−1)(n-1)-dimensional sphere instead of the nn-dimensional paraboloid (which is usually used to obtain results on Falconer’s problem), one can show that

∫Bn+1​(0,R)|ℰℙn​μ​(y)|2​𝑑ν​(y)\int_{B^{n+1}(0,R)}|\mathcal{E}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}\mu(y)|^{2}d\nu(y)

when μ\mu is an α1\alpha_{1}-Frostman measure on Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1) and ν\nu is an α2\alpha_{2}-Frostman measure on Bn+1​(0,R)B^{n+1}(0,R). Following the above arguments in the case k=1k=1, one can get slightly better bounds when the measure ν\nu is the appropriate rescaled version of ww (in other words, ν\nu is constant on lines through the origin). Obtaining improved bounds for general Frostman measures ν\nu would allow us to improve results for kk-stars, leading to improved results for graphs in general.

5. Nonempty Interior Results and Dimension Estimates

In this section, we adapt the methods used in the proof of the improved thresholds for positive measure of kk-stars in Theorem A to get nonempty interior and dimension estimates for kk-stars. We start by establishing Theorem B.

Remark 5.1.

The threshold we get for n=2n=2 and k=1k=1 is trivial. In fact, the L2L^{2} method strategy used above will never give something nontrivial for the nonempty interior problem in the plane. Indeed, if

𝒮​f​(x):=sup1≤t≤2|𝒜t​f​(x)|,{\mathcal{S}}f(x):=\sup_{1\leq t\leq 2}|\mathcal{A}_{t}f(x)|,

then an L2L^{2} bound

∫B⁡(0,1)∫12|∂t1/2+ϵ(dx)∗​f​(t)|2​𝑑t​𝑑x≲‖f‖L22\int_{B(0,1)}\int_{1}^{2}|\partial_{t}^{1/2+\epsilon}(d_{x})_{*}f(t)|^{2}\,dt\,dx\lesssim\|f\|_{L^{2}}^{2}

would imply that 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is bounded on L2L^{2} by Sobolev’s embedding. However, it is known that 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is not bounded on L2L^{2} in dimension 22.

As an application of Theorem B, we get Corollary 1.22, which brings some new information on the nonempty interior of pinned even necklaces.

Since both factors have nonempty interior, and products of open sets are open, it follows that

has nonempty interior in ℝ2​m\mathbb{R}^{2m}. This completes the induction. Applying the resulting chain statement to the decomposition of C2​lC_{2l} described above yields the desired conclusion for even cycles. ∎

Next, we move to dimension estimates for kk-stars. Given a set E⊂ℝnE\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} whose dimension is not large enough to apply Theorem A, that is dim(E)≤α+​(n,k)\dim(E)\leq\alpha_{+}(n,k), we investigate what dimensional lower bounds one can still get.

Appendix A Improvement of pinned nonempty interior for distances

In this appendix, we observe that estimates of Du–Zhang [6] yield improved thresholds for pinned nonempty interior of distance sets when n≥4n\geq 4, improving the best known thresholds from [3] for n≥4n\geq 4. That is the content of Theorem C, which we now prove.

Proof of Theorem C.

We provide a sketch of the proof since most of the arguments are standard. It is enough to show that for an α\alpha-Frostman measure μ1\mu_{1} in Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1) with support E1E_{1}, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for all smooth functions ff supported on Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1) whose support is a positive distance from E1E_{1}, one has

∫E1∫12|∂t1/2+ϵ𝒜t​f​(x1)|2​𝑑t​d​μ1​(x1)≲∫ℝn|ξ|α−n−ϵ​|f^​(ξ)|2​𝑑ξ\int_{E_{1}}\int_{1}^{2}|\partial_{t}^{1/2+\epsilon}\mathcal{A}_{t}f(x_{1})|^{2}\,dt\,d\mu_{1}(x_{1})\lesssim\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}|\xi|^{\alpha-n-\epsilon}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}\,d\xi

if

α>n⁡(n+1)2​n−1=n2+34+34​(2​n−1).\alpha>\frac{n(n+1)}{2n-1}=\frac{n}{2}+\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4(2n-1)}.

For j≥1j\geq 1, let 𝒫j\mathcal{P}_{j} be the Littlewood-Paley projection onto frequencies ≈2j\approx 2^{j} and for j=0j=0, let 𝒫0\mathcal{P}_{0} be the projection onto frequencies in Bn​(0,1)B^{n}(0,1). Write fj:=𝒫j​ff_{j}:=\mathcal{P}_{j}f.

We first split the left-hand side into the Littlewood-Paley pieces:

In the x1x_{1}-variable, since 𝒜t​f=f∗σt\mathcal{A}_{t}f=f*\sigma_{t} with σt\sigma_{t} denoting unnormalized surface measure on t​Sn−1tS^{n-1}, we have

=∫r≈2j∫E1|fj∗σ^r​(x1)|2​d​μ1​(x1)​rn−1​𝑑r\displaystyle=\int_{r\approx 2^{j}}\int_{E_{1}}|f_{j}*\widehat{\sigma}_{r}(x_{1})|^{2}d\mu_{1}(x_{1})\,r^{n-1}\,dr
≲∫r≈2j‖f^j‖L2​(r​Sn−1)2​r−α+αn​rn−1​𝑑r\displaystyle\lesssim\int_{r\approx 2^{j}}\|\widehat{f}_{j}\|_{L^{2}(rS^{n-1})}^{2}r^{-\alpha+\frac{\alpha}{n}}\,r^{n-1}\,dr
≈∫|ξ|≈2j|f^​(ξ)|2​|ξ|−α+αn​𝑑ξ.\displaystyle\approx\int_{|\xi|\approx 2^{j}}|\widehat{f}(\xi)|^{2}|\xi|^{-\alpha+\frac{\alpha}{n}}\,d\xi.

since

Applying this estimate to smooth approximations of a Frostman measure supported on the unpinned set and passing to the limit gives that the corresponding pinned distance measure has a density in H1/2+ϵ​(ℝ)H^{1/2+\epsilon}(\mathbb{R}), hence a continuous representative. Since the measure is nonzero, its support contains a nontrivial interval. ∎

Appendix B Application to Discrete Variants of kk-stars

Inspired by the proof of Corollary 1.5 in [14], we will prove the following corollary concerning finite point sets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. To our knowledge, this seems to be the first kk-star result in the discrete setting for k≥2k\geq 2 and may be of independent interest.

Corollary B.1 (Discrete pinned kk-stars).

Let 1≤k<n1\leq k<n, and let P⊂[0,1]nP\subset[0,1]^{n} be a set of NN points with mutual separation

|p−p′|≳N−1/n,p≠p′.|p-p^{\prime}|\gtrsim N^{-1/n},\qquad p\neq p^{\prime}.

Then for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist pins x1,…,xk∈Px_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in P such that

|Δx1,…,xkk​-star(P)|≳εNkα+​(n,k)−ε,\bigl|\Delta^{k\text{-star}}_{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}}(P)\bigr|\gtrsim_{\varepsilon}N^{\frac{k}{\alpha_{+}(n,k)}-\varepsilon},

where

α+​(n,k)=n2+n​k+k2​n+1.\alpha_{+}(n,k)=\frac{n^{2}+nk+k}{2n+1}.
Proof.

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. Choose ss with α+​(n,k)<s<n\alpha_{+}(n,k)<s<n and sufficiently close to α+​(n,k)\alpha_{+}(n,k) so that

ks>kα+​(n,k)−ε.\frac{k}{s}>\frac{k}{\alpha_{+}(n,k)}-\varepsilon.

Define the N−1/sN^{-1/s}-thickening of PP by

PN−1/s:=⋃p∈PB(p,N−1/s),P_{N^{-1/s}}:=\bigcup_{p\in P}B(p,N^{-1/s}),

and define the normalized measure

dμPs(x)=N−1Nn/s∑p∈PχB(p,N−1/s)(x)dx.d\mu_{P}^{s}(x)=N^{-1}N^{n/s}\sum_{p\in P}\chi_{B(p,N^{-1/s})}(x)\,dx.

We claim that μPs\mu_{P}^{s} is an ss-Frostman measure with constant independent of NN. Indeed, let B⁡(x,r)⊂ℝnB(x,r)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}. There are a few different possibilities for r>0r>0.

If 0<r≤N−1/s0<r\leq N^{-1/s}, then

μPs(B(x,r))≲N−1Nn/srn=(N−1/s)s−nrn≤rs,\mu_{P}^{s}(B(x,r))\lesssim N^{-1}N^{n/s}r^{n}=(N^{-1/s})^{s-n}r^{n}\leq r^{s},

since r≤N−1/sr\leq N^{-1/s} and s<ns<n.
